explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Disease elimination refers to the reduction to zero incidence of a specified disease in a defined geographical area as a result of deliberate public health efforts, although continued intervention measures are required to prevent re-establishment of transmission.

  • Even when no new cases occur in that region, the causative agent may still exist elsewhere, so ongoing measures such as vaccination, surveillance, vector control, or screening programs must continue to maintain elimination.
  • Therefore, elimination represents an intermediate stage between disease control and global eradication.
  • Elimination is usually achieved through high levels of herd immunity, strong surveillance systems, effective treatment of cases, and public health interventions that interrupt the chain of transmission.
  • Several diseases have been eliminated from specific countries or regions, although they may still exist elsewhere in the world.

Eradicated globally (Option B): Eradication refers to the permanent reduction to zero of the worldwide incidence of an infection, after which no further intervention measures are required. The classic example is smallpox, which has been eradicated globally.

Controlled (Option C): Disease control refers to the reduction of disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity, or mortality to a locally acceptable level through deliberate public health efforts. In this situation, the disease still occurs, but its impact is reduced and managed.

Reached the iceberg phenomenon (Option D): The iceberg phenomenon describes a situation in which the visible clinical cases represent only a small proportion of the total cases, while many infections remain subclinical, latent, or undiagnosed. It refers to the hidden disease burden rather than the absence of disease.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 46

ICD-11 introduced a new chapter on “Conditions related to sexual health,” to which gender incongruence has been moved from the mental disorders chapter.

  • This reclassification reflects the understanding that gender incongruence is not a mental health condition and helps reduce stigma associated with gender-related states.
  • ICD-11 was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2019 and came into effect on 1 January 2022.
  • It includes over 55,000 entities and about 120,000 clinical terms and was designed for digital health applications.
  • Important updates in ICD-11 include the new chapter on sexual health, a chapter on traditional medicine, reclassification of stroke as a neurological disorder, coding of allergy under diseases of the immune system, and the addition of addictive behaviours such as gaming disorder.

Traditional medicine (Option A): ICD-11 introduced a separate chapter for traditional medicine, mainly to classify diagnostic patterns used in traditional systems of medicine (such as Chinese, Japanese, and Korean medicine). Gender incongruence is not classified in this chapter.

Immune system disorders (Option C): This chapter includes conditions such as primary immunodeficiencies, autoimmune diseases, and allergies. Gender incongruence is unrelated to immune system disorders.

Addictive disorders (Option D): ICD-11 added new addictive behaviours, such as gaming disorder, under mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders. Gender incongruence was specifically removed from the mental disorders chapter and moved to the sexual health chapter instead.

Prescribing spectacles for refractive error is an example of tertiary prevention because it limits disability caused by an existing impairment.

  • Tertiary prevention includes all measures aimed at reducing or limiting impairments and disabilities and promoting adjustment to existing disease.
  • It is applied in the late pathogenesis phase when disease or impairment is already present.
  • Refractive error represents an impairment of visual function.
  • Without correction, this impairment can lead to disability, such as difficulty in reading or performing daily activities, and may eventually result in handicap, affecting social and occupational functioning.
  • Prescribing spectacles corrects the visual defect and restores functional ability, thereby limiting disability

Secondary prevention (Option B): Secondary prevention involves early diagnosis and prompt treatment of disease in its incipient stage, typically through screening and case-finding programmes. In this context, eye examination to detect refractive error represents secondary prevention.

Primary prevention (Option C): Primary prevention involves action taken prior to the onset of disease to prevent its occurrence. Examples include measures that promote general health or protect against specific diseases before they develop.

Health promotion (Option D): Health promotion refers to general measures aimed at improving overall health and well-being, such as health education and lifestyle improvement. It is not a targeted intervention to correct an established impairment.

Prevention of disability by appropriate treatment before disability occurs represents secondary prevention.

  • Secondary prevention involves early diagnosis and prompt treatment of disease at its incipient stage in order to halt disease progression and prevent complications.
  • By detecting disease early and providing adequate treatment, secondary prevention aims to arrest the disease process, restore health, and prevent complications such as disability.
  • Screening programmes and early treatment strategies are common interventions used in secondary prevention.
  • If disability has already developed, measures aimed at limiting disability and promoting rehabilitation fall under tertiary prevention.

Primary prevention (Option A): Primary prevention involves action taken before disease onset to remove the possibility that the disease will occur. It operates in the pre-pathogenesis phase and includes measures such as immunisation, sanitation, environmental protection, and lifestyle modification.

Tertiary prevention (Option C): Tertiary prevention is applied after the disease has progressed and aims to reduce impairments, limit disabilities, and promote rehabilitation, helping patients adjust to chronic or irreversible conditions.

Primordial prevention (Option D): Primordial prevention focuses on preventing the emergence of risk factors in populations where they have not yet appeared, often through individual and mass health education and broader lifestyle interventions.

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Pages 48, 50, 51

Explanation:

A Pap smear is an example of secondary prevention because it is a screening test used for early detection of cervical cancer and its precancerous lesions.

  • Secondary prevention is defined as an action that halts the progress of disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications.
  • The main interventions in secondary prevention are early diagnosis and adequate treatment, commonly achieved through screening tests and case-finding programmes.
  • Screening programmes such as Pap smear aim to detect unrecognised disease in asymptomatic individuals, when pathological changes have begun, but symptoms have not yet appeared.
  • Early detection and treatment help arrest the disease process, restore health, and prevent complications.
  • In many diseases, early diagnosis and treatment also reduce morbidity and mortality, and in infectious diseases, may reduce communicability, thereby protecting others in the community.
  • Thus, Pap smear screening represents secondary prevention, as it seeks out disease in its preclinical stage and allows timely intervention before progression to invasive cancer.

Primary prevention (Option A): Primary prevention refers to action taken prior to the onset of disease to remove the possibility that the disease will occur. It operates in the pre-pathogenesis phase and includes health promotion and specific protection, such as immunisation, sanitation, environmental protection, and lifestyle modification. For cervical cancer, HPV vaccination is an example of primary prevention.

Tertiary prevention (Option C): Tertiary prevention is applied when the disease has progressed beyond its early stages. It aims to reduce impairments and disabilities, minimise suffering, and promote rehabilitation, such as surgery, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy, in patients with established cervical cancer.

Primordial prevention (Option D): Primordial prevention focuses on preventing the emergence of risk factors in populations where they have not yet appeared. It often involves individual and mass health education, particularly directed toward children, to discourage harmful lifestyle habits that predispose to disease.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Pages 48-51, 448

Use of iodised salt is an example of primary prevention because it provides specific protection against iodine deficiency disorders before the disease occurs.

  • Primary prevention refers to action taken prior to the onset of disease to remove the possibility that the disease will occur.
  • It operates in the pre-pathogenesis phase and includes health promotion and specific protection measures.
  • Salt iodisation is a specific protective measure that supplies iodine to populations living in iodine-deficient areas, thereby preventing iodine deficiency disorders such as goitre and cretinism.
  • Since this intervention is applied before the disease develops, it represents primary prevention.

Primordial prevention (Option A): Primordial prevention aims to prevent the emergence of risk factors in populations where they have not yet appeared. It commonly involves lifestyle and environmental modifications, such as discouraging smoking or promoting healthy dietary habits from childhood.

Secondary prevention (Option C): Secondary prevention involves early diagnosis and prompt treatment of disease in its early or preclinical stage, usually through screening and case-finding programmes.

Tertiary prevention (Option D): Tertiary prevention is applied after the disease has progressed and aims to reduce impairments, limit disabilities, and promote rehabilitation, helping patients adjust to chronic or irreversible conditions.

Secondary prevention targets asymptomatic individuals with disease in the preclinical or incipient stage.

  • It is defined as an action that halts the progress of the disease at its early stage and prevents complications.
  • The main interventions include early diagnosis and prompt treatment, typically achieved through screening tests and case-finding programmes.
  • In secondary prevention, the aim is to detect unrecognised disease before symptoms appear, when pathological changes have begun but are still potentially reversible.
  • Early detection and adequate treatment can arrest disease progression, restore health, and prevent complications.
  • In infectious diseases, early diagnosis and treatment may also reduce communicability, thereby protecting others in the community.

Primary prevention (Option A): Primary prevention refers to action taken prior to the onset of disease to remove the possibility that the disease will occur. It operates in the pre-pathogenesis phase and includes health promotion and specific protection, such as immunisation, sanitation, environmental protection, and lifestyle modification.

Tertiary prevention (Option C): Tertiary prevention is applied when the disease process has progressed beyond its early stages. It aims to reduce impairments and disabilities, minimise suffering, and promote rehabilitation, helping patients adjust to chronic or irreversible conditions.

Primordial prevention (Option D): Primordial prevention focuses on preventing the emergence or development of risk factors in populations where they have not yet appeared. It is commonly achieved through individual and mass health education, especially among children, to discourage harmful lifestyle habits such as smoking, an unhealthy diet, and physical inactivity.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Primordial prevention is a concept receiving special attention in the prevention of chronic diseases.

  • It represents primary prevention in its purest sense, meaning the prevention of the emergence or development of risk factors in countries or population groups where they have not yet appeared.
  • Many adult diseases, such as coronary artery disease, obesity, and hypertension, have their early origins in childhood, as this is the stage when lifestyle habits such as smoking, eating patterns, and physical activity are formed.
  • Therefore, promoting healthy lifestyles from childhood aims to prevent the development of risk factors themselves.
  • In primordial prevention, efforts are directed toward discouraging children from adopting harmful lifestyles.
  • The main interventions include individual and mass health education, promoting healthy behaviours before risk factors appear.

Primary prevention (Option A): Primary prevention aims to prevent the onset of disease by controlling existing risk factors or increasing resistance to disease. It is applied before disease occurs but may involve individuals who already have risk factors, such as encouraging smoking cessation or treating hyperlipidaemia to prevent coronary artery disease.

Secondary prevention (Option B): Secondary prevention involves early diagnosis and prompt treatment of disease in its early stage to halt or slow its progression. Examples include screening programs such as blood pressure measurement or cancer screening.

Tertiary prevention (Option C): Tertiary prevention is applied after disease has developed and aims to limit disability and promote rehabilitation, such as cardiac rehabilitation following myocardial infarction or rehabilitation after stroke.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 48

Explanation:

  • Public health surveillance involves the systematic and continuous collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health-related data for public health action.
  • By observing trends in time, place, and persons, surveillance helps identify health problems and provides information needed for health planning, policy development, and evaluation of disease prevention and control programmes.
  • The final phase of surveillance is the application of this information to health promotion and disease prevention, and control.

Direct patient care (Option A): Surveillance focuses on population-level health information rather than providing clinical services to individual patients. Direct patient care is the responsibility of clinical medicine, not surveillance systems.

Individual diagnosis (Option C): Diagnosis refers to identifying a disease in an individual patient to guide treatment. Surveillance instead analyzes aggregated data to understand disease patterns and trends in populations.

Quarantine enforcement (Option D): Quarantine is a disease control measure applied to individuals exposed to communicable diseases. While surveillance data may guide decisions about quarantine during outbreaks, enforcement itself is an intervention and not a function of surveillance.



Reference:

question: Public health surveillance is preferentially aimed at:

correctAnswer: B. Identifying missing cases to supplement routine notifications
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Sentinel surveillance is used when routine disease notification systems fail to identify all cases of infection or disease.

  • It involves selected reporting units (such as interested and competent physicians or institutions) that report cases occurring in their areas.
  • This method helps identify missing or unreported cases, thereby supplementing routine notification systems.
  • Data obtained from sentinel sites may be extrapolated to estimate disease prevalence in the larger population.
  • Sentinel surveillance can minimise reporting bias and provide more detailed and reliable information than traditional notification systems.

Identifying cases free of disability (Option A): Surveillance is generally concerned with the presence of disease or the severity of disability (morbidity), not specifically identifying those who are healthy or "free of disability."

Directly treating patients (Option C): Like all forms of surveillance, sentinel surveillance is a data collection and analysis tool. While the clinics acting as sentinel sites do treat patients, the surveillance system itself does not provide treatment; it provides the information needed to plan where treatment resources should go.

Eradicating diseases (Option D): Eradication requires universal surveillance (active search for every single case) to ensure the pathogen is gone everywhere. Sentinel surveillance only looks at selected reporting sites rather than the entire population, which is insufficient for the total elimination or eradication of a disease.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 47

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Breaking the chain of transmission is not a direct function of surveillance.

  • Surveillance is defined as the systematic and continuous collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health-related data for use in planning, implementing, and evaluating public health practice.
  • Surveillance generates information that guides interventions such as isolation, treatment, immunisation, vector control, and environmental measures, which are the actions that actually interrupt disease transmission.
  • Thus, surveillance supports control measures but does not itself directly interrupt transmission.
  • The direct roles of surveillance include:
    • Providing information for health planning and policy decisions (Option A).
    • Identifying public health problems and potential disasters (Option B), including early detection of outbreaks through reporting systems and mortality data.
    • Detecting new and changing disease trends (Option D) by analysing patterns in time, place, and person.

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 47

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Monitoring refers to the performance and analysis of routine measurements aimed at detecting changes in the health status of a population or in environmental conditions.

  • It involves the regular observation and measurement of specific indicators to identify trends or deviations over time.
  • Monitoring helps assess whether health programs and environmental conditions are progressing as expected and allows early detection of unfavourable changes.
  • Common examples of monitoring include air pollution monitoring, water quality monitoring, growth monitoring in children, and monitoring of nutritional status.
  • These routine measurements help identify changes in health or environmental conditions so that appropriate public health actions can be taken when necessary.

Surveillance (Option A): Surveillance is the continuous and systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health data for the purpose of planning, implementing, and evaluating public health actions. It is broader than monitoring and is often described as “information for action.”

Sentinel surveillance (Option C): This is a special type of surveillance in which selected reporting sites such as particular hospitals or physicians collect data on specific diseases. It is used to monitor trends and detect early warning signals when universal surveillance is not feasible.

Systematic review (Option D): A systematic review is a research method used in evidence-based medicine that involves identifying, critically appraising, and synthesising results from multiple studies addressing a specific research question. It is not a method for routine measurement of population health status.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Pages 46, 47

Explanation:

Alzheimer’s disease is often described as the “silent epidemic of the century” because of its gradual onset, progressive course, and rapidly increasing prevalence worldwide, particularly with the ageing of populations.

  • The disease develops insidiously over many years, often without obvious early symptoms, and progressively leads to memory loss, cognitive decline, and impairment of daily functioning.
  • The term “silent epidemic” highlights the growing global burden of dementia, much of which is due to Alzheimer’s disease.
  • According to global estimates, over 55 million people worldwide live with dementia, and Alzheimer’s disease accounts for the majority of these cases.
  • The number of affected individuals is expected to rise substantially as life expectancy increases, making it a major public health challenge of the 21st century.

Hypertension (Option A): Hypertension is commonly referred to as the “silent killer” because it often produces no symptoms until serious complications such as stroke, heart disease, or kidney failure occur.

Diabetes (Option B): Diabetes mellitus is a major chronic disease with a large global burden, but it is not typically referred to as the silent epidemic of the century in standard epidemiological terminology.

Depression (Option D): Depression is a common mental health disorder and a leading cause of disability worldwide, but it is not commonly described by this specific term.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Herd immunity (also called community immunity) occurs when a large proportion of a population becomes immune to an infectious disease, usually through vaccination or previous infection, thereby providing indirect protection to individuals who are not immune.

  • When the number of immune individuals is sufficiently high, the chain of transmission is interrupted, making it difficult for the infectious agent to spread within the community.
  • For many vaccine-preventable diseases, achieving high levels of herd immunity is a key factor in disease elimination.
  • Herd immunity works by reducing the number of susceptible individuals in the population.
  • As a result, even if an infected person enters the community, the probability of transmitting the infection to susceptible individuals becomes low.
  • Immunisation programs are therefore the primary strategy used to build herd immunity and support disease elimination efforts.

Isolation (Option A): Isolation refers to the separation of infected persons during the period of communicability to prevent transmission to healthy individuals. Although useful in controlling spread, it is a case-based measure and alone cannot achieve population-level elimination.

Quarantine (Option B): Quarantine involves restricting the movement of healthy individuals who have been exposed to a communicable disease during the incubation period. It helps limit spread during outbreaks but is not the main long-term strategy for disease elimination.

Surveillance (Option D): Surveillance is the continuous, systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health data. It helps monitor disease trends and evaluate control programs, but it does not directly interrupt the transmission of infection.

Explanation:

Disease elimination refers to the reduction to zero incidence of a specified disease in a defined geographical area as a result of deliberate public health efforts, while continued intervention measures are required to prevent re-establishment of transmission.

  • Although new cases no longer occur in that region, the causative agent may still exist elsewhere, so ongoing control measures such as vaccination, surveillance, and public health interventions must continue to maintain the elimination status.
  • Thus, elimination represents an intermediate stage between disease control and eradication.

Eradication (Option A): This refers to the permanent reduction to zero of the worldwide incidence of an infection, after which continued intervention measures are no longer required. A classic example is smallpox, the only human disease successfully eradicated globally.

Control (Option C): Disease control refers to the reduction of incidence, prevalence, morbidity, or mortality of a disease to a locally acceptable level through deliberate public health efforts. Continued interventions are necessary to maintain this reduction.

Surveillance (Option D): Surveillance is the continuous, systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health data needed for planning, implementing, and evaluating public health practice. It is a monitoring tool, not a level of disease reduction.

correctAnswer: B. Accident - Disease; Loss of foot - Impairment; Cannot walk - Disability; Unemployed - Handicap
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The disability sequence described by WHO follows the progression: Disease → Impairment → Disability → Handicap. This sequence explains how a pathological event can lead to structural damage, functional limitation, and eventually social disadvantage.

  • Disease/Disorder:
    • This is the initial pathological event.
    • In this example, the accident represents the disease or disorder that initiates the sequence.
  • Impairment:
    • This refers to any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological, or anatomical structure or function.
    • The loss of a foot represents the structural abnormality caused by the accident.
  • Disability:
    • Disability is defined as any restriction or lack of ability to perform an activity in the manner considered normal for a human being.
    • The inability to walk represents the functional limitation resulting from the impairment.
  • Handicap:
    • Handicap refers to a social disadvantage resulting from an impairment or disability that limits or prevents the fulfilment of a normal role in society.
    • In this example, becoming unemployed represents the social consequence of the disability.


Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 50

Explanation:

Duration of illness is not a component of the epidemiological triad. It relates to the clinical course or natural history of the disease rather than the causal interaction between agent, host, and environment that determines disease occurrence.

  • The epidemiological triad is a model used to explain disease causation through the interaction of three key components: agent, host, and environment.
  • It emphasises that disease occurs due to the combined influence of these three factors rather than the agent alone.
  • Host factors (Option A):
    • These include characteristics that affect an individual's susceptibility to disease, such as malnutrition, immune status, age, genetic factors, and coexisting illnesses.
    • In tuberculosis, individuals with weakened immunity or poor nutritional status are more likely to develop active disease after infection.
  • Agent factors (Option B):
    • These refer to the specific causative organism responsible for the disease. In tuberculosis, the agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
    • Characteristics such as virulence, infectivity, and drug resistance influence the occurrence and severity of the disease.
  • Environmental factors (Option C):
    • These include external conditions that facilitate transmission of the disease.
    • For tuberculosis, important environmental factors include overcrowding, poor ventilation, poverty, and poor housing conditions, which increase the likelihood of airborne spread.


Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 39

If a patient seeks medical attention at an advanced stage of disease pathogenesis, the interventional approach shifts towards limiting disability. The primary goal is to prevent the progression from disease-induced impairment to a handicapped state.

The sequence of events leading to disability and handicap is as follows:

Disease → Impairment → Functional Limitation → Disability → Handicap

  • Disease is the initial pathological condition.
  • Impairment refers to a problem in body function or structure.
  • Functional Limitation is the restriction in performing fundamental physical actions.
  • Disability is the restriction or lack of ability to perform an activity in the manner considered normal for a human being.
  • Handicap refers to a disadvantage that limits or prevents the fulfilment of a normal social role for an individual.

question: Which of the following is not a healthcare delivery indicator?

correctAnswer: B. Ability to lead a socially and economically productive life
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The modern interpretation of the WHO definition emphasises the ability to lead a socially and economically productive life. This reflects the functional and dynamic concept of health beyond the mere absence of disease.

  • The WHO Constitution (1948) initially described health as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, moving beyond the mere absence of disease.
  • An operational definition was later needed for measurement purposes. In a broad sense, health was viewed as adequate functioning; in a narrow sense, as normal function without evidence of disease.
  • The modern modification highlights the crucial dimension of the ability to lead a socially and economically productive life, shifting the focus from a static “complete well-being” concept to a practical and functional resource for living.
  • Health is recognised as a fundamental human right, and well-being is considered an entitlement for all individuals.
  • Health is intersectoral and integral to development, meaning it is not solely the result of medical care but is influenced by social, economic, environmental, and political determinants.
  • Health is central to quality of life and is considered a major social investment, enabling individuals to contribute productively to society.
  • Maintaining health involves individual, state, and international responsibility, making it a global social goal rather than merely a personal concern.

Spiritual well-being (Option A):
Although spiritual health has been proposed as an additional dimension (notably discussed in WHO forums in 1998), it has not been formally incorporated into the official WHO definition.

Environmental well-being (Option C): Environmental factors are recognised as important determinants of health, but “environmental well-being” is not part of the formal WHO definition of health.

Genetic well-being (Option D): Genetics influence susceptibility to disease, but there is no recognised “genetic well-being” component in the WHO definition. Modern public health focuses on gene-environment interaction rather than defining a state of genetic health.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 14

question: According to the WHO definition, health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. In recent years, this definition has been modified to also include:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The germ theory of disease forms the basis of the biomedical concept. Postulated by Louis Pasteur (and later expanded by Robert Koch), it states that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.

  • The biomedical model views the human body as a biological machine, and disease as a deviation from normal structure or function. It emphasizes:
    • A specific causative agent
    • Pathological changes in tissues
    • Diagnosis and curative treatment
  • This model was highly successful in the control of infectious diseases and dominated medical thought in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
  • Limitations of the Biomedical Concept:
    • Focuses primarily on biological factors
    • Ignores social, psychological, environmental, and cultural determinants
    • Inadequate for explaining chronic diseases, malnutrition, lifestyle disorders, and environmental health problems

Ecological concept (Option A): Views disease as a disturbance in the dynamic equilibrium between agent, host, and environment. Disease results from maladjustment rather than a single causative germ.

Psychosocial concept (Option B): Recognises that health and disease are influenced by social, psychological, cultural, economic, and political factors, expanding beyond purely biological explanations.

Holistic concept (Option D): A synthesis of all models, viewing health as a multidimensional process involving physical, mental, and social well-being within the family, community, and environment. It emphasises intersectoral responsibility and health promotion.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 13

Disability indicators measure the impact of illness on functional ability, rather than simply the presence of disease or death.

  • Disability rates have emerged as crucial health indicators because death rates alone do not reflect the full impact of illness and injury.
  • These indicators are based on the premise that health implies the ability to perform a full range of daily activities.
  • Disability indicators are classified into two types:
    • Event-type indicators - measure specific events or periods of disability. These include:
      • Number of days of restricted activity
      • Bed disability days
      • Work-loss or school-loss days during a specified period
    • Person-type indicators - classify individuals based on their limitations, such as:
      • Limitation of mobility (e.g., confined to bed or house)
      • Limitation of activity, including the ability to perform activities of daily living (ADL) such as eating, washing, and dressing
  • In addition to disability indicators, broader composite measures of health status include:
    • HALE (Health-Adjusted Life Expectancy): Measures the equivalent number of years a person can expect to live in full health, adjusting life expectancy for time spent in poor health.
    • QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Years): Combines both quality and quantity of life lived; 1 QALY equals one year in perfect health.
    • DALY (Disability-Adjusted Life Years): Measures overall disease burden as the sum of years of life lost (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD).

Mortality indicator (Option A): Measures death rates in a population (e.g., crude death rate, infant mortality rate). It does not assess disability or functional status.

Morbidity indicator (Option B): Measures the occurrence of disease (incidence and prevalence). It reflects disease frequency, not the level of activity restriction caused by illness.

Health utilisation indicator (Option D): Measures the use of healthcare services (e.g., hospital admission rates, bed occupancy rate, immunisation coverage). It reflects service utilisation rather than individual health status.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 26

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

HALE (Health-Adjusted Life Expectancy) is defined as the average number of years that a newborn can expect to live in full health.

  • It is derived from life expectancy at birth but adjusts for time spent in states of less-than-full health, using current rates of ill health and mortality.
  • Thus, HALE reflects both the quantity and quality of life in a population.

Life expectancy at birth (Option A): This refers to the average number of years a newborn is expected to live if current mortality rates remain constant. It measures only the length of life and does not account for morbidity, disability, or reduced health states.

Disability-free life expectancy (Option C): Also known as active life expectancy or Sullivan’s Index, this measure estimates the expected years of life lived without disability. It generally uses a binary classification (disabled vs. not disabled) and therefore does not account for varying degrees of health states in the way HALE does.

Years lost to premature death (Option D): This refers to Years of Life Lost (YLL), which measures the mortality component of disease burden. YLL is one of the components used to calculate Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) and does not estimate expected healthy lifespan.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 26

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Proportional Mortality Rate (PMR) indicates the relative importance of a specific disease as a cause of death in a community.

  • It shows what proportion of the total deaths are due to a particular disease.
  • Proportional Mortality Rate = (Number of deaths due to a specific disease / Total number of deaths) × 100
  • Because it uses readily available mortality data and does not require population denominators, PMR is considered one of the simplest measures for estimating disease burden in a community.

Case fatality rate (Option A): This measures the killing power or severity of a disease. It represents the proportion of individuals with a particular disease who die from it. Thus, it reflects disease severity among affected individuals, not the overall burden of that disease in the community.

Incidence rate (Option B): This measures the number of new cases of a disease occurring in a population during a specified period. It indicates the risk of developing the disease but does not represent the mortality burden or the relative importance of the disease as a cause of death.

Proportional mortality rate (Option D): This represents the proportion of total deaths attributed to a specific cause. It is useful for comparing the relative contribution of different diseases to overall mortality, but it does not indicate the actual risk of dying from that disease in the population.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 25

Bed disability days are an event-type disability indicator that measures the number of days a person is confined to bed due to illness or injury, reflecting morbidity burden rather than service utilisation.

  • Health utilisation rates measure the extent to which health services are actually used by the population.
  • They are usually expressed as the proportion of people in need of a service who receive it during a specified period (commonly one year).
  • These indicators provide information about health service coverage and performance and indirectly reflect the health needs and health status of a population.
  • Utilization of health services is influenced not only by need but also by factors such as availability and accessibility of services, affordability, and the attitude of individuals toward health care and the health system.
  • Common examples of utilisation rates include:
    • Proportion of infants fully immunised (Option A) against vaccine-preventable diseases
    • Proportion of pregnant women receiving antenatal care (Option B)
    • Percentage of the population using family planning methods
    • Bed occupancy rate (Option D)
    • Average length of hospital stay (days of care rendered ÷ discharges)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Bed Turnover Interval (TOI) is the average time a hospital bed remains vacant between the discharge of one patient and the admission of the next patient.

  • It is an indicator of hospital bed utilisation and reflects how efficiently inpatient facilities are used.
    • Bed Turnover Interval = (Number of vacant bed days / Number of discharges)

  • For optimum utilisation of hospital services, the bed turnover interval should be low and slightly positive, allowing a short period for cleaning, preparation of the bed, and administrative arrangements before admitting the next patient, while avoiding unnecessary idle time of beds.

Zero interval (Option B): This would imply immediate admission after discharge, leaving no time for bed preparation or infection control measures.

Always negative (Option C): A negative turnover interval is not practically possible, since a bed cannot be occupied before it is vacated.

Maximised (Option D): A large turnover interval indicates that beds remain vacant for longer periods, reflecting under-utilisation of hospital resources.

Explanation:

Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is the ratio of deaths of infants under 1 year of age in a given year to the total number of live births in the same year, usually expressed per 1000 live births.

  • It is one of the most widely accepted indicators of health status, reflecting not only the health of infants but also the overall health status of a population and the socio-economic conditions under which people live.
  • Infant Mortality Rate = (Number of deaths of infants under 1 year of age in a given year / Number of live births in the same year) × 1000
  • IMR is also a sensitive indicator of the availability, utilisation, and effectiveness of health care services, particularly maternal and perinatal care.
  • Infant survival depends on several factors, including maternal health, antenatal care, safe delivery, newborn care, nutrition, sanitation, immunisation, and access to health services.
  • Because of these multiple determinants, IMR serves as a key indicator of the overall health and development of a community.

Crude death rate (Option A): This measures the total number of deaths in a population per year per 1000 population. It is strongly influenced by the age structure of the population, making it a relatively insensitive indicator of health status.

Under-5 mortality rate (Option C): This measures deaths among children below five years of age per 1000 live births. It reflects child survival and socio-economic conditions, but IMR is traditionally considered the more sensitive indicator of health care availability and effectiveness.

Maternal mortality rate (Option D): This measures maternal deaths related to pregnancy, childbirth, or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy per 100,000 live births. Although it reflects the quality of obstetric care and women’s health, it does not represent the overall health status of the entire population as comprehensively as IMR.

question: The best indicator of the availability, utilisation, and effectiveness of health care, and a very sensitive indicator of overall health status, is:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Years) is a measure that combines both the quantity of life gained and the quality of life during those years.

  • It is widely used in cost-utility analysis to assess the cost-effectiveness (value for money) of medical interventions.
  • In QALY calculations, each year of life is assigned a quality weight ranging from 1 (perfect health) to 0 (death).
  • Years lived with illness or disability are given values between 0 and 1 depending on the quality of health.
  • The benefit of an intervention is therefore measured as additional years of life gained, adjusted for the quality of those years.

DALY (Option A): Disability-Adjusted Life Years measure the burden of disease rather than the benefit of an intervention. DALY represents the total loss of healthy life due to disease and is calculated as:
DALY = Years of Life Lost (YLL) + Years Lived with Disability (YLD).

HALE (Option C): Health-Adjusted Life Expectancy is a population-level indicator that estimates the average number of years a person can expect to live in full health, adjusting life expectancy for time spent in poor health. It is not used to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of individual medical interventions.

PQLI (Option D): Physical Quality of Life Index is a social development indicator based on infant mortality rate, life expectancy at age one, and literacy rate. It reflects overall socio-economic development rather than the clinical effectiveness or economic value of medical treatments.

• The term "quarantine" originates from the Italian word "quaranta," meaning 40.
  • In the 14th century, during the outbreak of the bubonic plague, authorities in maritime cities like Venice implemented a rule that ships arriving from infected ports had to anchor for 40 days before passengers and crew could disembark.
  • This 40-day isolation period was chosen for religious and practical reasons, as it was believed to be long enough to determine whether someone had the disease.

Public health strategies:

  1. Isolation separates individuals who are already ill and potentially infectious from others for the maximum period of communicability to prevent disease spread. It can occur either in healthcare facilities or at home, depending on illness severity and resource availability. It is a defensive strategy.
  2. Quarantine separates and restricts the movement of individuals exposed to a contagious disease for a maximum known incubation period, but not yet symptomatic to monitor for symptoms and prevent potential disease spread upon becoming infectious.

Isolation and quarantine are examples of primary prevention.

  1. Social distancing is a public health measure involving maintaining physical distance and avoiding crowded places or gatherings. It aims to prevent the transmission of infectious diseases but applies broadly, not specifically to individuals already ill.
  2. Contact tracing is the process of identifying and monitoring individuals in close contact with an infected person. It is used to identify potential secondary cases and implement appropriate measures, such as quarantine or testing, to prevent further transmission.

Primordial prevention (Option A): is incorrect because primordial prevention focuses on preventing the development of risk factors in the first place, like promoting a healthy environment or addressing social determinants. While tobacco control laws aim to prevent smoking, they are more specifically aimed at reducing existing risk factors (tobacco use), making primary prevention a more accurate term.

Secondary prevention (Option C): is incorrect because secondary prevention focuses on early detection and intervention after the risk factors have been established. Tobacco control laws, however, aim to prevent the risk factor (tobacco use) from even emerging.

Tertiary prevention (Option D): is incorrect because tertiary prevention deals with management and rehabilitation of individuals who already have diseases or conditions, which is not the focus of tobacco control laws. These laws are intended to prevent the occurrence of tobacco-related diseases in the first place.

Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, Edition 26, Page 48, 49

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Years of potential life lost due to premature death.
  • Example: If a 30-year-old dies, potentially losing 45 years of life (assuming a life expectancy of 75).
  • YPLL is a mortality indicator, less sensitive in developed nations with better disease control.

Mortality indicators:

Crude death rate

CDR = (Total no. or deaths in a community/ MYP (Mid-year population) in the same area) x 100

  • The mid-year population is taken on 1st July
  • Limitation: It does not consider the age and sex of the population

Age-specific death rate

ASDR = (Total no. of deaths in a particular age group (eg. 20-24yrs) a given area in a year/ MYP of the age group in the same area and year) x 1000

Expectation of life
  • Life expectancy at birth: A positive mortality indicator· Average no. of years a newborn is expected to live, considering the current age-specific mortality rates in a community.
  • Important component to calculate the Human Development Index (HDI).
  • Life expectancy at one year is PQLI. In 2021, life expectancy in India is 69.7 years.

Infant mortality rate

IMR = (Total number of deaths (0-1-year-old) in a given year / Total number of live births in the same year) x 1000. It is a health status indicator.

Under-five mortality rate

U5MR = (Total number of deaths (0-5 years old) in a given year /Total number of live births in one year) x 1000

Maternal Mortality Rate

Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) = (Total no. of maternal deaths/women in the reproductive age group [15-49 years]) x 100,000

Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR)

Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) = (Total no. of maternal deaths/Live Births) x 100,000

Adult mortality rate

Probability of dying between 15 to 60 years of life

Year of potential life lost

Premature death measurement. If life expectancy is 75 years, and death happens at age 30, then 45 years of potential life is lost

Proportional mortality rate

The simplest measure of the burden of disease (Total deaths due to disease 'x'/ Total deaths in a community)́ x 100

Case fatality rate

CFR = (Deaths due to diseases ‘z’ / total no of cases of disease ‘z’) x 100

Disability Indicators:

Quality-adjusted Life Years (QALY)

(Option D ruled out)
  • Quality and quantity of life lived.
  • Assesses number of years of life added due to the intervention and hence the benefit and value for money of the intervention
  • QALY - 1 year of life lived in perfect health
  • Positive indicator of the cost-effectiveness of an intervention.
  • Scored between 0 (death) and 1 (perfect health).

Disability-adjusted Life Years (DALY)

(Option C ruled out)
  • DALY= Years of life lost to premature death + years lived with disability
  • 1 DALY: 1 year of healthy life lost
  • It is a measure of the burden of disease and the effectiveness of intervention

Year of life lost (YLL):

  • Calculated from the number of deaths at each age multiplied by the expected remaining years of life according to a global standard life expectancy.

Years lost to disability (YLD):

  • Where the number of incident cases due to injury and illness is multiplied by the average duration of the disease and a weighting factor reflecting the severity of the disease on a scale from 0 (perfect health) to 1 (dead).

DALY = YLL + YLD

Health Adjusted Life Expectancy (HALE)
  • The average number of years a newborn is expected to live in full health considering the current age-specific mortality rate.
    Healthy Life Expectancy
    • HALE = Life Expectancy at birth + adjustment of time spent in poor health
    • HALE = LE-DALY

Life Expectancy

  • Average no. of years a newborn is expected to live, considering the current age-specific mortality rate.

Sullivan’s index
(or DFLE)
  • Disability-free life expectancy (DFLE) with the current pattern of mortality and disability.

Years lost to morbidity (Option A): YPLL refers to premature death, not morbidity.



Reference:

Park’sTextbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27th ed pg 26, 64, 635

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Pearl Index is calculated as the number of pregnancies per 100 woman-years of exposure to a contraceptive method. It is a technique for evaluating contraceptive efficacy.

Formula

(Total accidental pregnancies / Total months of exposure) x 1200

Numerator

The total number of accidental pregnancies, including pregnancies that resulted in live births, stillbirths, abortions, or are ongoing.

Denominator

(Total months in the review period) – (months stopped using contraception for non-pregnancy reasons)

Minimum Data

At least 600 months of exposure.

Disadvantages
  • PI assumes a constant failure rate over time, but contraceptive failure rates typically decline with longer use.
  • High-fertility couples conceive earlier, skewing results towards lower-fertility couples later in studies.
  • PI ignores factors beyond accidental pregnancy that affect effectiveness, like user dissatisfaction, side effects, attempts to conceive, or loss of follow-up.

Better methods
  • Life Table Analysis is the preferred method for evaluating contraceptive efficacy.
  • It calculates interval-specific (monthly) failure rates and estimates the cumulative failure rate over time (12 or 24 months).


Reference:

Park’s Textbook of Preventive Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 585

Explanation:
The germ theory of disease forms the basis of the biomedical concept. Postulated by Louis Pasteur (and later expanded by Robert Koch), it states that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.

  • The biomedical model views the human body as a biological machine, and disease as a deviation from normal structure or function. It emphasizes:
    • A specific causative agent
    • Pathological changes in tissues
    • Diagnosis and curative treatment
  • This model was highly successful in the control of infectious diseases and dominated medical thought in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
  • Limitations of the Biomedical Concept:
    • Focuses primarily on biological factors
    • Ignores social, psychological, environmental, and cultural determinants
    • Inadequate for explaining chronic diseases, malnutrition, lifestyle disorders, and environmental health problems

Ecological concept (Option A): Views disease as a disturbance in the dynamic equilibrium between agent, host, and environment. Disease results from maladjustment rather than a single causative germ.

Psychosocial concept (Option B): Recognises that health and disease are influenced by social, psychological, cultural, economic, and political factors, expanding beyond purely biological explanations.

Holistic concept (Option D): A synthesis of all models, viewing health as a multidimensional process involving physical, mental, and social well-being within the family, community, and environment. It emphasises intersectoral responsibility and health promotion.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 13

explanationHtml:
Secondary prevention focuses on early detection and treatment of diseases to prevent complications. Colonoscopy is a screening tool used to detect colon cancer at an early, asymptomatic stage, allowing for timely intervention. Since the person has no prior screening but is at high risk due to family history, this falls under secondary prevention.


Levels of prevention

Definition

Primordial
  • Prevention of establishment of risk factors.
  • It aims to discourage people from adopting harmful habits.
  • Avoiding smoking

Primary
  • Health promotion and specific protection.
  • Prevention of onset of disease in a high-risk group/individual.
  • It aims to protect the health of those who are at risk.
  • Reduces the incidence of the disease.
  • Quit smoking

Secondary
  • Disease progression can be prevented at an early stage (Disease is reversible).
  • It aims to reduce the prevalence of the disease by early identification and prompt treatment of diseases, and it also prevents complications.
  • Screening for diabetes.

Tertiary
  • Prevention or limitation of impairment and disability in a diseased patient who has developed complications due to the disease and the disease has become irreversible.
  • It aims to minimize a patient's suffering and maximize potential years of useful life.
  • Disability limitation and rehabilitation.

Quaternary
  • Prevention of the risk of overmedicalization of a patient or population.
  • Aims to prevent prescription of unnecessary medications and invasive medical interventions.

Primordial (Option A) is incorrect because primordial prevention aims to prevent the emergence of risk factors by addressing social and environmental determinants, which is not applicable here.

Primary (Option B) is incorrect because primary prevention focuses on preventing disease before it occurs through interventions like vaccination, lifestyle modifications, or dietary changes. Screening tests do not fall under primary prevention.

Tertiary (Option D) is incorrect because tertiary prevention involves managing existing disease to prevent complications or disability, which applies to patients already diagnosed with colon cancer, not those undergoing screening.



Reference:

Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th edition, Pg 48, 49

Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) do not provide protection against breast cancer. In fact, some studies suggest that long-term use of OCPs may slightly increase the risk of breast cancer, especially in women with other risk factors.


Adverse Effects of Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs)

Contraindications of Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs)

Cardiovascular Effects (due to estrogen content)

  • Myocardial infarction (MI)
  • Cerebral thrombosis - Stroke
  • Risk increases with age >35 and cigarette smoking.

Carcinogenesis

  • Increased risk of cervical cancer

Metabolic Effects (due to progesterone content)

  • Elevated blood pressure
  • Altered serum lipid levels
  • Interference with blood clotting
  • Interference with carbohydrate metabolism

Thromboembolic Events

  • Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
  • Pulmonary embolism (PE)

Others

  • Lactation: Reduced quantity and quality of breast milk
  • Weight gain
  • Migraine
  • Breast tenderness

Absolute Contraindications:

  • Cancer of the breast and genitals
  • Liver disease
  • Previous or present history of thromboembolism
  • Cardiac abnormalities
  • Congenital hyperlipidaemia

Relative Contraindications (requiring medical surveillance):

  • Age over 40 years
  • Smoking and age over 35 years
  • Mild hypertension
  • Chronic renal disease
  • Migraine

Carcinoma endometrium (Option B) is incorrect because OCPs significantly reduce the risk of endometrial cancer by suppressing endometrial proliferation through progesterone action.

Colonic cancer (Option C) is incorrect because studies have shown that OCPs reduce the risk of colorectal cancer, although the exact mechanism is still being researched.

Ovarian cancer (Option D) is incorrect because OCPs provide strong protection against ovarian cancer by reducing ovulation frequency, which lowers the risk of malignant transformation in ovarian epithelial cells.

Prevalence refers to the total number of all existing cases (old + new) of a disease or attribute in a population at a given time or during a specified period, divided by the population at risk.

  • It is expressed as a proportion (or percentage)
  • Although often termed “prevalence rate,” it is technically a ratio/proportion, not a true rate
  • It represents a snapshot of disease burden in the population
  • Types:
    • Point prevalence: Cases at a specific point in time
    • Period prevalence: Cases over a defined time interval

A rate (Option A): A true rate includes a time component in the denominator

An incidence measure (Option C): Incidence measures new cases over time

A mortality measure (Option D): Mortality refers to deaths, not existing cases

Explanation:

Standardisation (direct or indirect) adjusts for differences in age distribution between populations, allowing fair comparison.

  • When comparing mortality between populations with different age compositions, the crude death rate is not a valid measure, because:
    • Rates are comparable only when the populations are comparable
    • Mortality is strongly influenced by age distribution
  • To overcome this, age standardisation (adjustment) is used:
    • It removes the confounding effect of age
    • Produces a single adjusted rate that allows direct comparison of mortality experience
  • Standardisation can also be done for other variables such as sex, race, and parity.

Methods of Standardisation:

  • Direct method: Applies age-specific rates of the study population to a standard population to obtain expected deaths and an adjusted rate
  • Indirect method (Standardised mortality ratio): Compares observed deaths with expected deaths based on a standard population

Crude death rate (Option A): Not comparable due to differing age structure

Case fatality rate (Option C): Measures disease severity

Definition of epidemiology (by John M Last ): Study of frequency, distribution and determinants of health-related states/events or disease in population groups and application of the study to control health problems.

Components of epidemiology:

question: Which of the following is an example of a ‘Rate’ in epidemiology?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In epidemiology, tools of measurement show disease frequency/magnitude. They are rate, ratio, and proportion.

  • Rate: Numerator/Denominator x 1000 or 10,000 or 1,00,000 where the numerator is a part of the denominator
  • Ratio: Numerator/Denominator where the numerator is not a part of the denominator
  • Proportion: Numerator/Denominator x 100 where the numerator is a part of the denominator

Definitions in Epidemiology

Measure Definition
Ratio A comparison of two numbers, e.g., male to female ratio
Proportion A type of ratio where the numerator is part of the denominator, e.g., % of infected
Rate A proportion with a time component, e.g., incidence rate per year

These are essential for calculating incidence, prevalence, case fatality rate, etc.

Tools for risk assessment (Option A): Incorrect because while rates and ratios are used in risk assessment, they are more fundamentally classified as measurement tools.

Tools for biostatistical analysis (Option B): Incorrect because this is too broad and indirect—while they are used in biostatistics, their primary role in epidemiology is measurement.

Measures of central tendency (Option D): Incorrect because central tendency refers to mean, median, and mode, not rate, ratio, or proportion.

Steps

Salient points

Verification of diagnosis
  • Most important step

3

Defining the population at risk
  • Obtain a map of the area affected.

4

Rapid search for all cases and their characteristics
  • Medical survey.
  • Epidemiological case sheet.

5

Data analysis
  • Done in terms of Time, Place and person
  • Try to identify the type of epidemic by drawing the epidemic curve.

6

Formulation of hypothesis

question: Which of the following is a characteristic of analytical study?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) is an experimental (interventional) study, also described as an epidemiological experiment, in which participants are randomly allocated into study and control groups.

  • It is considered the gold standard because it involves:
    • Randomisation → ensures comparability between groups and reduces bias
    • Manipulation (intervention) → deliberate application or withdrawal of an exposure
    • Follow-up → observation over time to assess outcomes
  • This design allows a more reliable assessment of the relationship between an intervention and an outcome.
  • However, randomisation reduces but does not eliminate bias, and additional methods such as blinding are used to further minimise bias.

Case-control study (Option A): This is an observational study that compares individuals with and without disease and assesses past exposure; it is more prone to bias.

Cohort study (Option C): This is an observational study that follows individuals over time; the absence of randomisation allows potential confounding.

Ecological study (Option D): This uses population-level data rather than individual data and provides weaker evidence for causality.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A prospective cohort study is one in which the outcome has not yet occurred at the start of the study, and participants are followed from the present into the future to observe the development of disease.

  • The study begins with a disease-free population, which is then classified based on exposure status and followed over time to compare the incidence of disease between groups.
  • Including individuals who already have the disease would:
    • Prevent measurement of new cases (incidence)
    • Violate the required temporal sequence (exposure must precede disease)
    • Distort the comparison between exposed and non-exposed groups
  • Thus, only individuals free of the outcome at baseline are eligible for inclusion in a prospective cohort study.

Individuals who are lost to follow-up (Option A): Loss to follow-up occurs after the study begins and cannot be identified at baseline.

Individuals who have a family history of IBD (Option B): These individuals are at increased risk and are important for studying exposure-disease relationships.

Individuals who withdraw consent (Option D): Withdrawal is a post-enrollment event, not a baseline exclusion criterion.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Relative risk (RR) is defined as the ratio of the incidence of disease (or death) among the exposed to that among the non-exposed

  • It is a direct measure of the strength of association between a suspected risk factor and disease, and is typically calculated in cohort studies.
  • Interpretation:
    • RR = 1 → no association
    • RR > 1 → positive association (risk factor)
    • RR < 1 → negative association (protective effect)
  • Quantitatively:
    • RR = 2 → 100% increase in risk
    • RR = 0.25 → 75% reduction in risk
  • The magnitude of RR reflects the strength of association, but it does not by itself imply causation.
  • Confidence intervals are often used to assess the precision and reliability of the estimate.

Odds ratio (Option A): Used in case-control studies, based on odds rather than incidence.

Attributable risk (Option B): Represents the difference in incidence between exposed and non-exposed groups.

Prevalence ratio (Option D): Used in cross-sectional studies, comparing existing cases rather than incidence.

  • ARR = 12% − 11% = 1%

Relative Risk (RR): This is the ratio of the risk in the treatment group compared to the control group.

  • RR = 11/12 = 0.916 (approx. 0.9)

Relative Risk Reduction (RRR): This explains how much of the baseline risk was removed by the treatment.

  • RRR = 1 − RR
  • RRR = 1 − 0.916 = 0.083 (approx. 10%)

Relative risk (Option A): A ratio of incidences (Ie / Iu), indicating strength of association rather than excess risk.

An Ecological study is an analytical observational study in which the unit of analysis is a group or population, rather than individuals.

  • In this study, both exposure (dietary practices) and outcome (mortality rates) are assessed using aggregate data at the regional level, not at the individual level. Hence, it is an ecological study.
  • Ecological studies are useful for identifying associations at the population level and are commonly used for hypothesis generation.

Case-control study (Option A): This involves comparing individuals with the disease (cases) and without the disease (controls) and assessing their past exposure.

Cohort study (Option B): This involves following a group of individuals over time to observe the occurrence of disease based on exposure status.

Randomised controlled trial (Option D): This involves random allocation of individuals into intervention and control groups to study the effect of an exposure.
