Explanation:

Reliability (repeatability / precision / reproducibility) is the ability of a test to give consistent results when repeated on the same individual or sample under identical conditions.

  • The repeatability of a test depends on observer variation, biological (subject) variation, and technical errors.
  • For example, measurement of blood pressure is often poorly reproducible due to the influence of these factors.
  • A test may be reliable but not valid, meaning it produces consistent results that are not necessarily close to the true value.

Validity (Option A): Refers to the accuracy of the test, i.e., its ability to measure the true value, usually by comparison with a gold standard.

Sensitivity (Option C): A measure of validity indicating the ability to correctly identify individuals with the disease (true positives).

Specificity (Option D): A measure of validity indicating the ability to correctly identify individuals without the disease (true negatives).

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 154

High validity and low reliability (Option B): Results would be close to the true value on average but show wide variation on repeated testing.

Low validity and low reliability (Option D): Results would be both inaccurate and inconsistent, with wide variation and deviation from the true value.

Specificity is calculated using the formula:

Step 1: Identify the given values

  • Subclinical case:

A subclinical case is one where an individual is infected with a disease but doesn't show any apparent symptoms. However, they can still transmit the disease to others. This is important in epidemiology because these cases can silently spread infections.

  • Primary case:

It is the first case of a disease identified in a group or population. This case introduces the disease to a previously unaffected population and is often the source of an outbreak.

  • Secondary case:

It results from direct contact with a primary case. These individuals contract the disease from the primary case, representing the spread of the infection within the population.

  • Index case:

It is the first case that health authorities have noticed. It's important to note that the index case is not always the same as the primary case. Sometimes, health authorities might identify a case that turns out to have been infected by an earlier, previously undetected case.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A basic reproduction number (R0) >1 signifies that the infection has epidemic potential.

The basic reproduction number (R0) is a crucial metric in epidemiology that helps to understand the potential for an infectious disease to spread within a population. Biological, sociobehavioral, and environmental factors influence it.

R0 > 1:

  • It indicates that each infected individual transmits the infection to more than one person.
  • It suggests that the disease has the potential to cause an epidemic, as the number of infections is likely to increase over time.

R0 < 1:

  • It indicates that each infected individual transmits the infection to less than one person.
  • It suggests the infection will likely decline and eventually die out in the population.

R0 = 1:

  • It indicates each infected individual transmits the infection to precisely one other person.
  • It suggests a stable state where the infection is endemic; it persists in the population without causing an outbreak.

https://www.cebm.net/covid-19/when-will-it-be-over-an-introduction-to-viral-reproduction-numbers-r0-and-re/

Explanation:

The median incubation period is the time for 50% of cases to show symptoms after exposure.

  • The incubation period is the time between infection and the first symptom appearance.
  • During incubation, the pathogen multiplies until it reaches a threshold to cause symptoms.
  • Most diseases aren't communicable during incubation, except for measles and chickenpox.
  • Incubation periods vary by disease and individual, ranging from hours to years.
  • Examples:
    • Short (hours to days): Food poisoning, cholera.
    • Medium (10 days to 3 weeks): Typhoid, COVID-19, measles.
    • Long (weeks to years): Hepatitis, Rabies, leprosy.
  • Non-infectious diseases like cancer also have incubation periods, often lasting months or years.

Shortest time from exposure to symptom onset in 50% of cases (Option A) describes the minimum incubation period, not the median.


Longest time from exposure to symptom onset in 50% of cases (Option B) describes the maximum incubation period, not the median.


Average time from exposure to recovery in 50% of cases (Option C) describes the average recovery time, not the incubation period.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Serial Interval:

  • It is the duration between the onset of symptoms in a primary case (the first person infected in a chain of transmission) and the onset of symptoms in secondary cases (people infected by the primary case).
  • It helps epidemiologists understand how quickly a disease spreads from one person to another within a community or population.

Incubation Period:

  • The incubation period refers to the time it takes for an individual to develop symptoms after being infected with a pathogen.
  • It begins with exposure to the pathogen and ends with the appearance of recognisable symptoms.

Window Period:

  • The window period is the time between infection and when the infection can be reliably detected by diagnostic tests.
  • The individual may be infectious during this period, but tests might not yet show positive results.
  • This concept is important in screening and testing strategies for infectious diseases.

Generation Time:

  • Generation time refers to the time the newly infected person takes to show symptoms.
  • It encompasses the entire cycle of infection, transmission, and symptom onset in the context of disease spread.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pertussis (whooping cough) is a highly contagious acute respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis. In susceptible unimmunized household contacts, the secondary attack rate averages approximately 90%, highlighting its exceptional transmissibility.

  • This very high attack rate is due to the fact that pertussis is most infectious during the catarrhal stage (Option D), the earliest phase of illness, when patients have mild fever, coryza, sneezing, and an irritating cough that resembles a common cold.
  • Because diagnosis is often missed at this stage, infected individuals continue normal close contact and efficiently spread infection within households.
  • The bacilli are transmitted mainly through respiratory droplets expelled during coughing, sneezing, or talking, and humans are the only reservoir.
  • Importantly, there is no chronic carrier state and no significant subclinical infection contributing to spread (Option C), so transmission occurs almost exclusively from symptomatic cases, including mild or unrecognised infections.
  • This explains why pertussis can spread rapidly among unvaccinated children and why timely immunisation is critical for disease control.

The incubation period usually exceeds 4 weeks (Option A): This is incorrect because the incubation period is usually 7-14 days, and generally does not exceed 3 weeks.

Explanation:

According to INDEX-TB and WHO recommendations, adjunct corticosteroids are specifically indicated in HIV-negative patients with tuberculous meningitis and tuberculous pericarditis, where excessive inflammatory response can lead to serious complications.

  • In TB meningitis, corticosteroids reduce cerebral edema, intracranial pressure, vasculitis, and neurological complications, thereby lowering mortality and long-term neurological sequelae.
  • In TB pericarditis, steroids help reduce inflammation, decrease pericardial effusion, and lower the risk of developing constrictive pericarditis.
  • Steroids are given along with standard anti-tubercular therapy and are usually tapered over several weeks depending on the clinical condition and regimen used.

question: A patient with drug-resistant tuberculosis is being evaluated for inclusion in a bedaquiline-based treatment program. Which of the following patients is not eligible for bedaquiline therapy under standard conditional access criteria?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

According to current programmatic guidelines, the longer all-oral M/XDR-TB regimen has a total duration of 18-20 months, with XDR-TB patients typically requiring the full 20 months with appropriate modifications.

  • The regimen commonly includes drugs such as Linezolid, Clofazimine, Cycloserine (continued for the entire duration) along with Levofloxacin and Bedaquiline, where Bedaquiline is given for the initial 6 months and may be extended in selected cases.
  • Treatment duration is guided by culture conversion and clinical response, and in most patients, therapy continues for 15-17 months after culture conversion within the total 18-20 month period.
  • This prolonged duration is necessary because drug-resistant TB involves limited effective drugs and slower bacterial clearance, requiring sustained multidrug therapy to prevent relapse and further resistance.

12 months (Option A): This duration is insufficient for XDR-TB and is shorter than the recommended longer oral regimen duration.

6 months (Option C): This is the standard duration for drug-susceptible TB and is entirely inadequate for drug-resistant TB.

24 months (Option D): Older regimens sometimes extended up to 24 months, but current guidelines standardize the longer oral regimen to 18-20 months, with a maximum around 20 months in most cases.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 227

Explanation:

In a patient who is sputum smear-positive, tuberculosis is microbiologically evident regardless of chest X-ray findings, as radiographic changes may be absent in early or minimal disease.

  • According to current TB diagnostic algorithms under national programs, the next step is CBNAAT (Cartridge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) to provide rapid molecular confirmation and, more importantly, detect rifampicin resistance.
  • This aligns with the principle of Universal Drug Susceptibility Testing (UDST), where every diagnosed TB case should undergo resistance testing before or at the time of treatment initiation.
  • Early identification of drug resistance is critical to avoid inappropriate therapy and improve outcomes.

Start empirical ATT (Option A): Although smear positivity suggests TB, starting treatment without drug resistance information is not preferred under current guidelines when CBNAAT is available.

Repeat chest X-ray after 1 week (Option C): A normal chest X-ray does not exclude pulmonary TB in a smear-positive patient, and repeating imaging does not contribute to microbiological confirmation or resistance detection.

Perform Quantiferon test (Option D): This test is used for latent TB infection and has no role in diagnosing or managing active pulmonary TB in a smear-positive patient.

question: A 42-year-old man presents with chronic cough for 4 weeks, evening fever, and weight loss. Sputum smear microscopy shows acid-fast bacilli. However, his chest X-ray is reported as normal with no radiographic abnormalities. What is the next best step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

CBNAAT (Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test) is the most rapid molecular diagnostic test for pulmonary tuberculosis because it detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA directly from clinical specimens within about 2 hours using automated nucleic acid amplification technology.

  • A major advantage of CBNAAT is its ability to simultaneously detect rifampicin resistance, which serves as an important marker for multidrug-resistant TB and enables early initiation of appropriate therapy.
  • This combination of speed, high sensitivity, specificity, and drug-resistance detection makes CBNAAT the preferred frontline rapid molecular test in modern TB diagnostic algorithms.
  • Unlike conventional diagnostic methods, CBNAAT does not require bacterial growth in culture, which significantly shortens diagnostic time.
  • It is especially valuable in smear-negative, paucibacillary, and high-risk drug-resistant TB cases.

Sputum smear microscopy (Option A): This is a rapid conventional screening test but is not a molecular method, has lower sensitivity, and cannot detect drug resistance.

Interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) (Option C): IGRA is used mainly for detecting latent TB infection and cannot reliably diagnose active pulmonary TB or assess drug resistance.

Liquid culture using BACTEC system (Option D): Although highly sensitive and useful for culture confirmation and drug susceptibility testing, it requires days to weeks for growth detection and is not the most rapid diagnostic option.



Reference:

https://ntep.in/node/398/CP-cbnaat-xpert-mtbrif-assaycartridge
question: The most rapid diagnosis of pulmonary TB can be done by:

correctAnswer: B. Flexor surface of the left forearm, midway between elbow and wrist
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Mantoux test is performed by injecting 1 TU of PPD in 0.1 mL intradermally on the flexor surface of the left forearm, midway between the elbow and wrist, which is the standard recommended site.

  • The injection is given using a tuberculin syringe with the bevel facing upward. If correctly administered, it produces a pale wheal measuring 6-10 mm, confirming proper intradermal placement.
  • This standardized site ensures uniform technique and reliable subsequent measurement of induration, which is read after 48-96 hours, ideally at 72 hours.
  • An induration measuring more than 10 mm is considered positive, indicating that the person has been infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis at some point in the past or present.

Dorsum of the hand (Option A): This is not a standard site for Mantoux testing and is not recommended for routine tuberculin skin test administration.

Deltoid region (Option C): The deltoid region is commonly used for BCG vaccination, but it is not the standard site for Mantoux intradermal testing.

Anterior thigh (Option D): This is not a recognized standard site for tuberculin skin testing in clinical practice.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 216

options.text: Flexor surface of the left forearm, midway between elbow and wrist

question: The Mantoux test is carried out by injecting PPD intradermally on the:

correctAnswer: C. Positive tuberculin test indicating past or present TB infection
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the Mantoux test, the result is interpreted by measuring the transverse diameter of induration (not erythema) at 48-96 hours, ideally at 72 hours after intradermal PPD injection.

  • In the Mantoux test, 1 TU of PPD in 0.1 mL is injected intradermally on the flexor surface of the left forearm, midway between the elbow and wrist.
  • An induration measuring more than 10 mm is considered positive, indicating that the person has been infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis at some point in the past or present.
  • A positive Mantoux test reflects a delayed Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to tuberculoprotein and indicates immune sensitization, but it does not distinguish between latent and active disease.

False positive reaction (Option A): An induration of 12 mm exceeds the standard positive threshold and is therefore interpreted as a true positive reaction unless specific confounding factors are identified.

BCG immunization only (Option B): Prior BCG vaccination may sometimes cause Mantoux reactivity, but a positive test cannot be assumed to be due to BCG alone without clinical correlation.

Definitive evidence of active pulmonary tuberculosis (Option D): A positive Mantoux test indicates TB exposure or infection only; it does not by itself confirm active tuberculosis disease



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 216

In infants aged 2 months up to 12 months, a respiratory rate of 50 breaths per minute or more (≥50/min) indicates fast breathing and is classified as pneumonia.

  • This age-based approach improves early identification of pneumonia, especially in primary care and community settings where radiologic confirmation is unavailable.
  • IMNCI respiratory cut-offs are based on the normal decline in respiratory rate with increasing age.

    • >40/min (Option B) in a child aged 12 months upto 5 years.

question: According to IMNCI, which respiratory rate cut-offs classify pneumonia in an infant aged 2 months to 12 months?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Under IMNCI, fast breathing is one of the most important clinical signs for classifying pneumonia in children with cough or difficult breathing.

  • Since radiological facilities may not be available in primary care settings, IMNCI relies on simple observable signs that can be assessed quickly by health workers.
  • Respiratory rate is counted for one full minute, and age-specific cut-offs are used:
    • <2 months: ≥60 breaths/minute
    • 2 months to 12 months: ≥50 breaths/minute
    • 12 months to 5 years: ≥40 breaths/minute
  • If a child with cough or difficult breathing has fast breathing, the child is classified as having pneumonia.
  • If chest indrawing or danger signs are also present, the classification becomes more severe.
  • This makes fast breathing a critical early diagnostic marker for timely recognition and treatment of pneumonia in community and primary healthcare settings.

Nasal flaring (Option A): Nasal flaring may indicate respiratory distress, but it is not the primary IMNCI criterion used for pneumonia classification.

Wheezing (Option B): Wheezing is more suggestive of airway obstruction, such as bronchiolitis or asthma, and is not the defining IMNCI sign for pneumonia classification.

Chest pain (Option C): Chest pain is not used as a standard IMNCI criterion for classifying pneumonia in children.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 187, 188

Explanation:

Before starting immunosuppressive therapy, a two-step tuberculin skin test is used to distinguish between a boosted reaction from prior exposure to tuberculosis and a new infection. This approach helps confirm a positive TST result, preventing unnecessary treatment for latent tuberculosis due to misinterpretation.

  • 1st test - read within 48 to 72 hours
    • If positive, consider the patient infected.
    • If negative, 2nd test after 3 weeks.
  • 2nd test - read within 48 to 72 hours - done after 3 weeks.
    • Positive - infected
    • Negative - uninfected

  • To confirm a recent positive TST result(Option B): That would be a repeat single TST, not a two-step test.

  • To monitor the effectiveness of immunosuppressive therapy on latent tuberculosis(Option D): TST is not used to monitor treatment effectiveness. Also, immunosuppression can cause false negatives in TST.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

While clinical interventions save individuals, Health education is the cornerstone of long-term cholera prevention and control at the population level. It bridges the gap between providing infrastructure (like toilets and clean water) and the actual behavioural change required to break the transmission cycle.

Key components of effective health education in a cholera-prone community include:

  • Handwashing: Teaching the critical times for handwashing with soap (after using the toilet, before preparing food).
  • Food Safety: Promoting the Boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it rule.
  • Water Treatment: Instructing families on how to use chlorine tablets or the boiling method to ensure drinking water is safe.
  • Early Recognition: Teaching the community to identify the signs of severe dehydration and start Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) immediately at home before seeking medical help.

The prophylactic measures against cholera include:

  • Health education
  • Food hygiene practices
  • Hand washing practices after defecation
  • Drinking safe water
  • Knowledge about ORS

Mass administration of antibiotics (Option A): Mass chemoprophylaxis is not recommended for cholera control. It is short-lived and leads to antibiotic resistance.

Closing all public markets (Option C): While food sanitation is vital, closing markets is a socioeconomic disruption that does not solve underlying issues.

Mandatory hospitalisation of all citizens (Option D): Hospitalisation is only for those requiring medical intervention for dehydration.

Among the human hookworms, Ancylostoma duodenale is more pathogenic because it causes greater intestinal blood loss per worm than Necator americanus, making it more likely to produce severe iron-deficiency anaemia in moderate to heavy infestations.

  • Hookworms attach to the mucosa of the small intestine, suck blood, and secrete anticoagulants, resulting in continued bleeding even after they detach.
  • Chronic hookworm infection leads to:
    • Persistent blood loss and depletion of body iron stores
    • Iron-deficiency microcytic hypochromic anaemia
    • Retarded growth and development in children
    • Reduced work capacity in adults
    • In pregnant women: increased morbidity, abortion, stillbirth, low birth weight babies, and impaired lactation
  • This chronic anaemia is especially severe in malnourished individuals and populations living in endemic tropical regions with repeated reinfection.

Necator americanus (Option B): Also causes blood loss, but less per worm than A. duodenale, making it less severe comparatively.

Strongyloides stercoralis (Option D): Causes intestinal and disseminated disease but is not a major cause of chronic hookworm-type blood loss anaemia.

Explanation:

Chloramphenicol, although historically used in acute typhoid fever, is not effective for clearing the chronic carrier state and is considered unreliable for eradication. Instead, prolonged courses of drugs such as ampicillin or amoxicillin are preferred.

  • Chronic typhoid carriers are epidemiologically important because they continue to excrete Salmonella typhi and act as persistent reservoirs of infection in the community.
  • In most chronic carriers, the organism persists in the gallbladder and biliary tract, especially in individuals with gallstones or biliary disease.
  • Because of this localisation, eradication is difficult, and in resistant cases, cholecystectomy combined with antibiotic therapy is often the most successful treatment approach.

The gallbladder is the most common site of persistence of Salmonella typhi (Option A): This is true; the biliary tract is the principal reservoir in chronic carriers.

Chronic carriers are an important source of community transmission (Option B): This is true because carriers serve as long-term reservoirs and may trigger outbreaks.

Cholecystectomy may be required in refractory chronic carriers (Option D): This is true; surgery may be necessary when antibiotic therapy alone fails.

correctAnswer: C. Plain glucose and dextrose solutions
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Plain glucose and dextrose solutions should not be used for the initial resuscitation of severe dehydration or shock because they do not stay in the intravascular compartment effectively and can worsen the hyperosmolar state. Ringer's Lactate or Hartmann's solution is the best commercially available choice.

In the management of shock or severe dehydration, the goal is volume expansion of the intravascular space (the blood vessels).

  • When you infuse a plain dextrose solution (like 5% Dextrose), the body quickly metabolises the glucose. What remains is free water.
  • Free water does not stay inside the blood vessels. It distributes itself throughout the entire body's water compartments, including the inside of cells. Only about 1/12th of the infused dextrose solution remains in the intravascular space.
  • Using dextrose for resuscitation fails to raise blood pressure effectively and can lead to cerebral oedema (swelling of the brain) because the free water rushes into brain cells.

Ringer's Lactate (Option A): Ringer's Lactate is the preferred fluid for initial intravenous rehydration in patients with shock or severe dehydration.

Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl) (Option B): While it is the "poorest" of the suitable fluids (as it doesn't correct acidosis or potassium loss), it is still a crystalloid that can be used if nothing else is available, unlike plain dextrose.

Hartmann's Solution (Option D): Hartmann's solution is a type of Ringer's Lactate and is highly recommended for the initial treatment of severe dehydration.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 272.
question: In the initial resuscitation of a patient with shock or severe dehydration, which of the following fluids should be avoided, as they do not effectively correct the condition?

correctAnswer: C. Return of skin elasticity and pulse strength
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Skin elasticity and pulse strength are the most helpful clinical indicators for monitoring adequate intravenous rehydration. The initial rehydration phase should be fast until an easily palpable pulse is present.

The initial rehydration must be fast until an easily palpable pulse is present. Reassess the patient every 1-2 hours.

  • After 1-2 litres of fluid have been infused, the drip should be slowed down till the blood pressure and pulse return to normal.
  • Rehydration must be continued until all signs of dehydration have disappeared. ORS should be given when the patient can drink oral fluids.

Puffy eyelids are a sign of excess rehydration, and intravenous fluids must be stopped when it occurs.

Unchanged urine output for 4 hours (Option A): Urine output may remain unchanged even after 3-4 hours of adequate rehydration; therefore, it cannot be used as a primary criterion for continuous assessment in the early phase.

Development of puffy eyelids (Option B): Puffy eyelids are actually a sign of excess rehydration (overhydration), signalling that intravenous fluids must be stopped immediately.

Decrease in blood pressure (Option D): A decrease in blood pressure is a sign of worsening shock or ongoing dehydration, not an indicator of successful rehydration.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 272.

correctAnswer: B. Rice water with added salt
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Home-based fluids that contain salt are recommended for preventing dehydration. These include rice water, unsalted soup, or yoghurt drinks, provided 3g/litre of salt is added.

If a simple sugar-salt solution is made at home, it should consist of 1 teaspoon of salt and 6 teaspoons of sugar dissolved in 1 litre of drinking water.

  • Fluids that do not contain salt in water, for eg: rice water, unsalted soup, yoghurt drinks, green coconut water, etc, are not preferred, although they may be used in cases where fluids that contain salt are unavailable. 3g/litre of salt must be added to such drinks before giving them to the child with diarrhoea.
  • The infant's usual diet of cereals, vegetables and other foods should be continued and never diluted. The child should be given as much nutrient-rich food as is acceptable.
  • Avoid the following:
    • Sweetened drinks with sugar, like commercial fruit juices and sweetened tea, as they lead to osmotic diarrhoea and hypernatremia (Option A ruled out)
    • Fluids with a stimulant and purgative effect, like coffee and medicinal tea infusions. (Option C ruled out)
    • Concentrated undiluted glucose solution (Option D ruled out): High concentrations of sugar in the gut lumen draw more water out of the body (osmotic effect), further dehydrating the patient.

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Pages 271, 272.

question: According to WHO guidelines for Oral Rehydration Therapy, what is the approximate volume of ORS solution required during the first 4 hours for a child weighing 12 kg?

correctAnswer: B. Oral or Intravenous rehydration therapy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In acute diarrhoea, the primary cause of death is not the infection itself, but dehydration and hypovolemic shock resulting from the massive loss of water and electrolytes.

  • Rehydration therapy is the gold standard of management. Most children (about 90%) with mild to moderate dehydration can be successfully treated with Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS).
  • ORS uses the glucose-sodium co-transport mechanism in the small intestine to pull water back into the body, even while diarrhoea is occurring.
  • Intravenous (IV) Fluids: These are reserved for children with severe dehydration, those in shock, or those who cannot drink due to persistent vomiting or altered consciousness. Ringer's Lactate is the preferred IV fluid.

Immediate administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics (Option A): Most pediatric diarrhoea is viral. Antibiotics are only secondary for specific bacterial cases.

Stopping all breastfeeding and solid food (Option C): Nutritional maintenance is vital for recovery. Breastfeeding should never be stopped. Breastfeeding should be continued more frequently during diarrhoea to provide both hydration and essential nutrients/antibodies.

Administration of anti-motility agents like Loperamide (Option D): Anti-motility agents can cause serious complications in children, such as paralytic ileus.

Classification

Signs

Treatment Plan

Severe Dehydration

Lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, skin pinch goes back very slowly (> 2 seconds).

Plan C: Immediate IV fluids.

Some Dehydration

Restless/irritable, drinks eagerly, sunken eyes, skin pinch goes back slowly.

Plan B: ORS in a supervised setting.

No Dehydration

Well, alert, skin pinch goes back immediately.

Plan A: Home-based fluids and continued feeding.

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 271.

Administration of anti-motility agents like Loperamide

question: In the management of a child with acute diarrhoea, which of the following is the most critical intervention to prevent mortality?

correctAnswer: B. Reported daily and weekly until the area is declared free of cholera
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In line with surveillance protocols, the number of cases and deaths due to cholera must be reported daily and weekly to health authorities until the area is officially declared free of the disease.

  • Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 24 hours of its occurrence.
  • When twice the incubation period (5 days), i.e. 10 days, has elapsed since the death, recovery, or isolation of the last case, an area is declared free of cholera.
  • Mass prophylaxis is not advised in cholera, as it fails to stop the spread of the disease. Chemoprophylaxis is only advised for household contacts or a closed community.

Reported once a month to the local police (Option A): This is incorrect because reporting needs to be frequent for outbreak response, and health departments are the relevant reporting body.

Kept confidential to prevent loss of tourism (Option C): This is incorrect as it violates international health transparency protocols.

Reported only if more than 1,000 deaths occur (Option D): This is incorrect because every confirmed case must be reported to ensure rapid containment.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 279.

Reported daily and weekly until the area is declared free of cholera
Kept confidential to prevent loss of tourism
Reported only if more than 1,000 deaths occur

question: According to the International Health Regulations, how should the reporting of cholera cases and deaths be managed during an outbreak?

correctAnswer: A. Coal tar disinfectant with a high RW coefficient
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most effective disinfectant for cholera stool is a coal tar disinfectant (like cresol) with a Riedel-Walker (RW) coefficient of 10 or more.

  • Bleaching powder may also be used if it is of good quality.
  • For disinfection, attention should be paid to the following: the patient's stools and vomit; clothes and other contaminated personal items; the latrine, the patient's house, and the neighbourhood.

Rideal-Walker (RW) Coefficient: This is a measure of a disinfectant’s killing power compared to phenol. A "high RW coefficient" indicates that the disinfectant is significantly more potent than standard phenol, making it suitable for heavy-duty disinfection of organic waste like faeces.

UV light exposure for 10 minutes (Option B): UV light cannot penetrate bulk waste like stool or vomit effectively enough to ensure total disinfection.

Scented aerosol sprays (Option C): These products are designed for odour masking and do not have the germicidal properties required to kill Vibrio cholerae.

Boiling water for 5 seconds (Option D): While heat is effective, a 5-second exposure is insufficient for large volumes of contaminated material.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 280.

options.text: Coal tar disinfectant with a high RW coefficient

question: Which of the following is considered the most effective disinfectant for the treatment of cholera stools and vomit?

correctAnswer: B. Safe water supply and sanitation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Safe water supply and sanitation are the first steps to be taken to decrease the incidence of cholera. Steps include ensuring a safe water supply and proper excreta disposal.

Steps taken to decrease the incidence of cholera include:

  • Safe water supply
  • Excreta disposal
  • Food sanitation
  • Disinfection
  • Early case detection

Mass chemoprophylaxis is not recommended for the control of cholera. This is because the drug's effect is only short-lived (a few days). Moreover, for preventing 1 case of cholera, around 10,000 individuals must be given the drug. Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for only household contacts of confirmed cases with tetracycline.

Cholera Vaccines: Available in oral forms

  • Dukoral
  • Sanchol and mORCVAX
  • Euvichol
    • Sanchol and Euvichol are available for mass vaccination campaigns. The campaigns have been implemented in areas experiencing an outbreak, in areas at heightened vulnerability during humanitarian crises, and among populations living in highly endemic areas, known as hotspots.
  • Vaxchora:
    • Vaxchora is given for adults (18 to 64 years) who are travelling to an area of active cholera transmission, at least 10 days before the trip.
  • CVD103-HgR - no longer produced

Distribution of oral vaccines to all children (Option A): This is incorrect because while vaccines like Shanchol are available, they are secondary to the primary goal of providing clean water.

Routine blood testing of the entire population (Option C): This is incorrect because cholera is diagnosed via stool analysis. Mass blood screening is not an effective way to decrease incidence.

Spraying of pesticides in residential areas (Option D): This is incorrect because cholera is not a vector-borne disease. Pesticides target insects, whereas cholera is prevented through water and sanitation.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Pages 279, 280.

options.text: Distribution of oral vaccines to all children
Routine blood testing of the entire population
Spraying of pesticides in residential areas

question: To decrease the incidence of cholera in an endemic area, what is considered the primary first step in environmental sanitation?

correctAnswer: C. Early initiation of physiotherapy with supportive devices
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Physiotherapy is vital for disability limitation → strengthens weakened muscles, prevents contractures, and improves functional recovery
  • Early initiation in affected limbs helps maximise recovery and minimise permanent disability
  • Use of metal callipers (orthotic support) assists mobility and prevents deformities

Management of Paralytic Polio:

  • No specific treatment exists → management focuses on supportive care and rehabilitation
  • Physiotherapy should begin early to help regain muscle strength
  • Residual paralysis can persist → rehabilitation is key to limiting long-term disability
  • Good nursing care + physiotherapy can prevent crippling sequelae

Disability limitation principles in polio:

  • Prevent muscle wasting and deformities
  • Maintain joint mobility and function
  • Promote independence in movement
  • Use assistive devices (e.g., callipers) for ambulation

Immediate administration of antiviral drugs (Option A): No antiviral therapy exists for polio; treatment is supportive

Prolonged rigid immobilisation of the affected limb (Option B): Immobilisation worsens muscle atrophy and joint stiffness

Administration of normal human immunoglobulin (Option D): Immunoglobulin is only useful before infection, not after symptom onset



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 248

options.text: Prolonged rigid immobilisation of the affected limb
Early initiation of physiotherapy with supportive devices

question: A 3-year-old child is recovering from paralytic poliomyelitis and has residual weakness in the lower limb. Which of the following interventions is most important to improve muscle strength and reduce long-term disability?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Tetracycline is the drug of choice for the chemoprophylaxis of cholera. It effectively reduces the secondary attack rate by inhibiting the multiplication of Vibrio cholerae in the gut.

  • It should be given for:
    • Adults: 3 days in a twice-daily dose of 500mg
    • Children (4-13 years): 125mg
    • Children (0-3 years): 50mg
  • Alternatively, the long-acting tetracycline (doxycycline) may be used for chemoprophylaxis if the prevailing strains are not resistant. A single oral dose of doxycycline (300 mg for adults and 6 mg/kg for children under 15 years) has proved to be effective.
  • Chemoprophylaxis is advised only for household contacts or a closed community in which cholera has occurred.

Streptomycin (Option B): Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside used for conditions like Tuberculosis or Plague. It is not effective against Vibrio cholerae in the gut lumen.

Penicillin G (Option C): Penicillin G is primarily effective against Gram-positive organisms. Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative organism.

Albendazole (Option D): Albendazole is an anthelmintic medication used to treat parasitic worm infestations. It has no antibacterial activity.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 280.
question: In a community experiencing a cholera outbreak, what is the drug of choice for the chemoprophylaxis of household contacts of confirmed cases?

correctAnswer: A. Suspect antibiotic resistance and prioritise immediate rehydration therapy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In cholera management, rehydration is the cornerstone of treatment and must be started immediately. Antibiotics are used to reduce the duration and volume of diarrhoea. However, if diarrhoea persists beyond 48 hours of therapy, resistance to the drug should be suspected.
  • Vibrio cholerae strains, particularly the O1 El Tor biotype, have shown increasing resistance to common drugs in various regions.

Treatment:

  • Rehydration therapy is started immediately, either oral or intravenous.
  • Antibiotic therapy - As soon as vomiting has stopped (usually after 3-4 hours of rehydration). Fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, azithromycin, ampicillin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are commonly used.
  • Antidiarrhoeals, cardiotonics, antiemetics, antispasmodics, and corticosteroids are not used.
  • Shock in diarrhoea must be corrected by intravenous fluids only.

Suspect co-infection with Rotavirus and start antiviral therapy (Option B): Rotavirus is a viral cause of diarrhoea, typically seen in younger children, and does not respond to the antibiotics used for cholera.

Suspect antibiotic resistance and prioritise high-dose corticosteroids (Option C): Corticosteroids are not used in the treatment of cholera. They have no role in managing secretory diarrhoea and can potentially worsen the patient's condition.

Suspect intestinal perforation and prioritise immediate surgical consult (Option D): Cholera causes a secretory diarrhoea through toxin-mediated mechanisms and does not typically lead to bowel perforation.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Pages 279, 280.

options.text: Suspect antibiotic resistance and prioritise immediate rehydration therapy
Suspect co-infection with Rotavirus and start antiviral therapy
Suspect antibiotic resistance and prioritise high-dose corticosteroids
Suspect intestinal perforation and prioritise immediate surgical consult

question: A patient presents with rice-water stools and severe dehydration, confirmed as cholera. Despite 48 hours of antibiotic therapy, the diarrhoea persists. What is the most likely clinical suspicion and the immediate priority in management?

correctAnswer: B. Acute diarrhoea with blood or pus
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The symptoms described, fever, abdominal cramps, and small-volume stools with blood and mucus, point to Dysentery. Unlike watery diarrhoea, which is caused by the loss of fluid and electrolytes from the small intestine, dysentery is caused by invasive pathogens that attack the lining of the large intestine (colon).
  • Shigella infection classically causes acute inflammatory diarrhoea with blood and pus, due to mucosal invasion and ulceration of the colon

Shigellosis:

  • Shigella causes bacillary dysentery → invasion of colonic mucosa
  • Leads to:
    • Bloody stools (hematochezia)
    • Pus (neutrophils in stool)
    • Tenesmus and abdominal cramps
  • Stool is typically small-volume and frequent, unlike watery diarrhoea
  • Reflects enteric infection pattern in your PDF: invasive pathogens → inflammatory (bloody) diarrhoea

Clinical relevance:

  • Differentiates from non-invasive diarrhoea (e.g., cholera, rotavirus)
  • Indicates colonic involvement and mucosal damage

Copious watery stool resembling rice water (Option A): “Rice-water stool” is classic for cholera, not invasive dysentery.

Scanty “pea soup” diarrhoea (Option C): “Pea soup” stool is associated with typhoid fever. Typhoid typically presents with prolonged fever and "rose spots" rather than the acute bloody stools of dysentery.

Pale, bulky, foul-smelling steatorrhea (Option D): Steatorrhea suggests malabsorption (e.g., giardiasis, Celiac disease, or chronic pancreatitis). The stools are pale, oily, and float, but do not typically contain blood.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Pages 269, 272, 273

options.text: Copious watery stool resembling rice water
Acute diarrhoea with blood or pus

question: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, abdominal cramps, and frequent small-volume stools containing visible blood and mucus. Which of the following best describes the typical stool finding in this infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A convalescent cholera carrier continues to excrete vibrios for about 2-3 weeks after recovery, contributing to transmission

Convalescent cholera carrier:

  • Carriers are classified into:
    • Incubatory carriers → short duration (early phase)
    • Contact (healthy) carriers → <10 days
    • Convalescent carriers → 2-3 weeks after illness
    • Chronic carriers → rare, prolonged excretion
  • During convalescence, patients are asymptomatic but still shed organisms in stool
  • An important source of infection in the continuation and spread of the outbreak
  • Reflects your PDF principle: faecal shedding and carrier states sustain transmission in enteric diseases

Public health relevance:

  • Identifying and managing carriers helps in breaking the faecal-oral transmission cycle
  • Emphasises the importance of sanitation and surveillance even after recovery

1-5 days (Option A): Core High-Risk Group (HRG).

Less than 10 days (Option B): Core HRG with the highest transmission risk.

6-8 weeks (Option D): Core HRG due to needle-sharing transmission



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 276
question: A 30-year-old man recently recovered from an episode of acute cholera. During follow-up, he is found to still be excreting Vibrio cholerae in his stool despite being asymptomatic. For how long does a convalescent cholera carrier typically continue to shed the organism?

correctAnswer: C. Bacteriological examination of purged stool after oral magnesium sulphate
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cholera carriers excrete low numbers of vibrios, so detection is improved by purging stool using magnesium sulphate, which increases organism yield for bacteriological examination

Cholera carriers:

  • Carriers are asymptomatic but can transmit infection via faecal shedding
  • Vibrios are present in lower concentrations than in clinical cases → routine stool exam may miss them
  • Purged stool technique (using 30-60g MgSO₄ orally) increases intestinal evacuation → improves detection
  • Cholera remains a non-invasive intestinal infection, with organisms confined to the gut lumen
  • Reflects enteric disease dynamics in your PDF: faecal shedding and carrier states play a role in transmission

Public health relevance:

  • Identifying carriers is important in outbreak control and surveillance
  • Helps break transmission chains in endemic and epidemic settings

Routine blood cultures during the febrile phase (Option A): Used in outbreak control of JE (fogging)

Examination of vomitus by dark-field microscopy (Option B): Larvicide used historically for mosquito control

Serological testing for antitoxin antibodies (Option D): Organophosphate larvicide for mosquito larvae.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 276.

options.text: Routine blood cultures during the febrile phase
Examination of vomitus by dark-field microscopy
Bacteriological examination of purged stool after oral magnesium sulphate

question: During a cholera outbreak investigation, asymptomatic individuals are screened to identify potential carriers. Because carriers excrete fewer organisms than symptomatic patients, which method is most effective for detecting Vibrio cholerae in these individuals?

correctAnswer: B. Live attenuated vaccine administered orally
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Rotavirus vaccines (e.g., Rotarix, RotaTeq) are live attenuated vaccines given orally, mimicking natural gut infection to induce mucosal immunity

Rotavirus vaccine:

  • Vaccines are designed to replicate in the intestine → induce local (IgA) + systemic immunity
  • Two main types:
    • Rotarix → monovalent human strain
    • RotaTeq → pentavalent bovine-human reassortant
  • Oral route is essential because infection is enteric (gut-based)
  • Reflects principles from your PDF: enteric infections are best prevented by vaccines inducing intestinal immunity

Public health importance:

  • Prevents severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants
  • Reduces hospitalisations and mortality, especially in developing countries
  • Complements (but does not replace) sanitation measures

Inactivated whole-cell vaccine given intramuscularly (Option A): Not inactivated; live vaccine is needed for mucosal immunity

Purified subunit vaccine given subcutaneously (Option C): Subunit vaccines do not induce strong intestinal immunity

Toxoid vaccine administered intradermally (Option D): Toxoid vaccines are used for toxin-mediated diseases (e.g., tetanus)



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Pages 273, 274.
question: A 2-month-old infant is brought for routine immunisation. The paediatrician plans to administer a vaccine that protects against severe diarrheal disease caused by rotavirus. Which of the following best describes the type and route of this vaccine?

correctAnswer: C. Predominant person-to-person and fomite transmission with high viral shedding
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The scenario describes an outbreak of Rotavirus, which is the most common cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhoea in children worldwide.
  • Rotavirus spreads mainly via person-to-person (faeco-oral) and fomites, with massive viral shedding, making hygiene and clean water alone insufficient to stop transmission

Rotavirus transmission:

  • Virus is shed in very high concentrations in stool → highly infectious
  • Transmission occurs via:
    • Direct person-to-person contact
    • Contaminated surfaces (fomites) like toys, hands
  • Even with improved sanitation, close contact settings (e.g., daycare) sustain transmission
  • Reflects enteric infection dynamics in your PDF: faeco-oral spread persists despite hygiene due to environmental contamination and high infectivity

Epidemiological features:

  • Nearly universal infection in early childhood
  • The major cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants
  • Control relies more on vaccination than on sanitation alone

Transmission via aerosolised respiratory droplets (Option A): Not respiratory; transmission is faeco-oral, not droplet-based

Infection limited to immunocompromised individuals (Option B): Affects almost all children, not just immunocompromised

Exclusive food-borne transmission resistant to boiling (Option D): Not exclusively food-borne; spread is mainly person-to-person



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 269.

options.text: Predominant person-to-person and fomite transmission with high viral shedding
Exclusive food-borne transmission resistant to boiling

question: A 1-year-old child presents with acute watery diarrhoea and vomiting. Several children in the daycare centre have similar symptoms despite adequate sanitation and access to clean drinking water. What best explains the continued high transmission of the causative organism?

correctAnswer: B. Current or former injecting drug users, even with a single past exposure
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

HCV screening is strongly recommended for anyone with a history of injecting drug use, even a single exposure → due to the high risk of blood-borne transmission

HCV screening:

  • HCV is primarily transmitted via parenteral exposure (infected blood, needles)
  • Screening is risk-based, targeting high-risk populations rather than universal age groups
  • High-risk groups include:
    • Injecting drug users (current or past)
    • Recipients of unscreened blood transfusions
    • Patients on long-term haemodialysis
    • People living with HIV
  • Many infections are asymptomatic → screening is essential for early detection
  • Reflects broader communicable disease strategy from your PDF: identify high-risk groups for targeted intervention

Clinical significance:

  • Early detection prevents progression to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Allows timely initiation of direct-acting antiviral therapy

Individuals consuming raw or undercooked shellfish (Option A): These relate to faeco-oral transmission (HAV/HEV), not blood-borne HCV

Travellers to areas endemic for enteroviruses (Option C): These relate to faeco-oral transmission (HAV/HEV), not blood-borne HCV

Healthcare workers working only in psychiatric wards (Option D): Risk depends on blood exposure, not specific workplace setting



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 265

options.text: Individuals consuming raw or undercooked shellfish
Current or former injecting drug users, even with a single past exposure
Travellers to areas endemic for enteroviruses
Healthcare workers working only in psychiatric wards

question: A 40-year-old man presents for a routine health check-up. He reports a history of injecting drug use once during his early 20s, but has been asymptomatic since. Which of the following individuals should be specifically recommended for Hepatitis C virus (HCV) screening?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hepatitis B vaccine must be given within 24 hours of birth → critical to prevent perinatal transmission and chronic carrier state

Vaccination in newborns of HBV patients:

  • Perinatal transmission occurs during delivery via exposure to maternal blood/body fluids
  • Early vaccination acts as post-exposure prophylaxis for the newborn
  • In high-risk settings, birth dose is mandatory regardless of maternal status
  • Often combined with HBIG (within 12-24 hours) for maximum protection
  • Prevents progression to chronic HBV infection, which is common in neonates
  • Reflects communicable disease prevention principles (early immunisation to block transmission)

Public health importance:

  • Neonates have a very high risk of chronicity (~90%) if infected
  • Birth dose significantly reduces vertical transmission and long-term disease burden

Within 6 hours after birth (Option A): The 6-hour window applies more strictly to HBIG; the vaccine window is up to 24 hours.

Within 48 hours after birth (Option C): Delay beyond 24 hours increases risk of infection and chronic carriage.

Within 7 days after birth (Option D): Delay beyond 24 hours increases risk of infection and chronic carriage.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 258.
question: A full-term newborn is delivered to a mother who is HBsAg-positive in a region with high rates of perinatal Hepatitis B transmission. What is the maximum recommended time window for administering the first dose of the Hepatitis B vaccine to prevent neonatal infection?

correctAnswer: C. Simultaneous administration of HBIG and Hepatitis B vaccine
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Combined HBIG + Hepatitis B vaccine (passive-active immunization) is ideal → provides immediate protection (HBIG) + long-term immunity (vaccine)

Needlestick injury - HBV:

  • HBV is transmitted via parenteral exposure (blood, needles) → high risk in healthcare settings
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) must be initiated as early as possible (preferably within 6-48 hours)
  • HBIG → provides immediate neutralising antibodies
  • Vaccine → induces active immunity for long-term protection
  • The combined approach is more effective than either alone
  • Reflects general communicable disease control principles in your PDF (early intervention + immunisation)

Clinical & preventive importance:

  • Prevents the establishment of infection after exposure
  • Especially critical when the source is HBsAg-positive
  • Standard protocol in occupational exposure guidelines

Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) alone within 7 days (Option A): HBIG alone gives only temporary protection; must be combined with vaccine and given early (not 7 days)

Hepatitis B vaccine alone within 48 hours (Option B): The vaccine alone is too slow; it lacks immediate passive immunity

Immediate initiation of oral antivirals (tenofovir/entecavir) (Option D): Antivirals are for chronic HBV management, not post-exposure prophylaxis



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 259

options.text: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) alone within 7 days
Hepatitis B vaccine alone within 48 hours
Simultaneous administration of HBIG and Hepatitis B vaccine

question: A 26-year-old healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury while drawing blood from a patient known to be HBsAg-positive. What is the most appropriate immediate post-exposure prophylaxis?

correctAnswer: B. Late incubation period and early symptomatic phase
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • HAV shedding in faeces is maximum during the late incubation period and early acute phase, making patients highly infectious even before jaundice appears

Hepatitis A in faeces:

  • Virus replicates in hepatocytes → excreted via bile → reaches intestine → shed in stool
  • Peak faecal shedding occurs before and just after symptom onset
  • Explains high transmissibility in community outbreaks (silent spreaders before jaundice)
  • As highlighted in the enteric infections in your PDF, faecal shedding drives faeco-oral transmission cycles

Clinical correlation:

  • Infectivity is highest before jaundice → important for outbreak control
  • Once jaundice appears → viral shedding declines rapidly
  • Shedding usually stops within ~1-2 weeks after the onset of jaundice

Public health significance:

  • Early-phase patients act as hidden reservoirs
  • Emphasises the importance of sanitation, hygiene, and water safety

Immediately after exposure, before hepatic replication (Option A): Virus must replicate in the liver first; shedding is not immediate.

Peak of jaundice with hepatic injury (Option C): Shedding decreases once jaundice appears; infectivity declines

Convalescent phase after symptom resolution (Option D): Minimal to no shedding during recovery phase



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 253

options.text: Immediately after exposure, before hepatic replication
Late incubation period and early symptomatic phase
Peak of jaundice with hepatic injury

question: A 10-year-old boy presents with fever, malaise, and jaundice. Several cases have been reported in his community due to contaminated water. At which stage of his illness is he most likely to be highly infectious due to maximal viral shedding in faeces?

correctAnswer: B. Faecal-oral transmission via contaminated food and water
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation (fever, jaundice) combined with the epidemiological setting (outbreak in a rural community following water contamination) is a classic description of Hepatitis A or Hepatitis E.

  • Hepatitis A virus (HAV) & Hepatitis E virus (HEV) are primarily transmitted via the faeco-oral route, especially through contaminated water and food
  • Common in areas with poor sanitation and hygiene, leading to outbreaks

Epidemiological relevance:

  • High prevalence in children in developing countries
  • Often causes community outbreaks linked to contaminated water supply
  • Hepatitis A is very common in children, while Hepatitis E often causes more severe outbreaks in young adults and is particularly dangerous for pregnant women.

Hepatitis viruses differ in transmission:

  • HBV, HCV → parenteral, sexual, vertical
  • HAV, HEV → faeco-oral route

Parenteral transmission via contaminated needles (Option A): Parenteral spread is typical of HBV/HCV, not HAV (only rare during viraemia)

Vertical transmission from mother to fetus (Option C): Vertical transmission is characteristic of HBV, not HAV

Sexual transmission via vaginal fluids (Option D): Sexual transmission is not the primary route; limited to specific practices (oral-anal)



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 253

options.text: Faecal-oral transmission via contaminated food and water
Vertical transmission from mother to fetus

question: A 6-year-old child from a rural area presents with fever, malaise, and jaundice. Several children in the same community have similar symptoms after consuming contaminated drinking water. What is the most likely mode of transmission of the causative virus?

correctAnswer: C. A. aegypti, being a discordant feeder, results in clustering and generation of multiple dengue cases
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Epidemiology of Dengue:

Agent factors
  • Infection with any one serotype (DENV-1, 2, 3, and 4) confers lifelong immunity to that virus serotype (No cross-immunity)
  • Secondary infection with serotype 2 or multiple infections with different serotypes leads to severe immunological catastrophe. (DHF/DSS)

Vector

1. Aedes aegypti:

  • Less aggressive
  • Nervous feeder, discordant feeder (needs >1 feed): clustering of dengue cases (Option C)
  • Striped body appearance
  • Breed: Stagnant artificial water collections like tires, pots, buckets, etc.(Option A)
  • Flight range: Short range-100 meters.
  • Eggs: single and cigar-shaped
  • Larvae: siphon tube

2. Aedes albopictus:

  • More aggressive
  • Concordant feeder (1 feed is enough)

Disease transmission
  • Infective stage:
  • Reservoir:
    1. Man: day before symptom onset to 5th day
    2. Mosquito: remain infective lifetime (transovarial transmission)
  • Transmission cycle: Man-mosquito-man
  • Incubation period: 3 to 10 days

Host Factors
  • Children have a milder disease than adults.(Option D)
  • High risk: infants, elderly, obese, pregnant, peptic ulcer disease, menstrual disease, congenital disease, hemolytic diseases, NSAIDs.

Environmental Factors
  • Temperature - 16 to 300C (Option B)
  • Endophagic and endophilic mosquitoes are influenced by a 2°C temperature rise, which shortens their extrinsic incubation period. Rural spread is linked to water projects, better transport, and water scarcity.



Reference:

Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Pg 290, 291

question: Which of the following factors is true regarding the spread of dengue infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A rapid antigen detection test (NS1) is used to diagnose dengue fever within 5 days of onset of fever. Dengue presents with high fever, severe headache, joint pain (breakbone fever), rash, and a positive tourniquet test. Laboratory findings often show leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes.

Blood culture (Option B) is not used to diagnose dengue fever, as it is a viral infection, not bacterial.

PCR for malaria (Option C) parasites is used to diagnose malaria. The patient presents with a shorter-duration fever and hepatosplenomegaly, not with a positive tourniquet test.

IgM ELISA (Option D) is used to diagnose dengue after >5 days of symptoms.



Reference:

Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 291-294

question: A 23-year-old woman presents with 3 days of high fever, headache, and joint pain. Examination reveals a maculopapular rash and a positive tourniquet test. Labs show leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and mildly elevated liver enzymes. What is the most appropriate next step for diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Larval Surveillance (density of larvae in the area)

Sampling unit: Houses or premises searched for water-holding containers.

House index: Number of houses positive for aedes larvae/number of houses searched.

Container index: Number of containers positive/ number of containers checked.

Breteau index: The number of positive containers, and the number of houses checked.

  • Most sensitive to assess endemicity

Aedes Aegypti Index:

  • Percentage of houses and their premises showing actual breeding of A. aegypti larvae.
  • Should not be >1%
  • Airports and seaports in endemic areas should be kept at least 400m around their premises free from the breeding of Aedes aegypti.


Reference:

question: All of the following are true about larval surveillance?

correctAnswer: B. Aerosol mode transmission is not reported in India
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

question: A 10-year-old boy was bitten on the forearm by a stray dog. The bite wound is superficial with mild bleeding. Based on the Indian rabies management guidelines, which of the following is not recommended for this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Administer two doses of rabies vaccine on days 0 and 3.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The management of re-exposure depends on the timing and nature of previous vaccinations.

1. Re-Exposure Prophylaxis within 3 Months:

If a patient who has been bitten by an animal suspected to be rabid has completed a full rabies vaccination series within the last three months.

  • No Further Vaccination Required:
    • The immune response from the initial series is still strong, providing sufficient protection.
    • If necessary, only the wound should be cleaned thoroughly, and tetanus prophylaxis should be considered.

2. Re-Exposure Prophylaxis After 3 Months:

  • Wound Care on day 0
  • Administration of Two Booster Doses of the rabies vaccine.
    • Day 0: first dose.
    • Day 3: Second dose.
    • This booster regimen helps to reinforce the patient's immunity, ensuring continued protection against the rabies virus.
  • Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG):
    • RIG is not required for patients who have previously completed a rabies vaccination series.
    • RIG is typically reserved for those who have never been vaccinated or have incomplete vaccination histories.


Reference:

Contraindications:

  • No contraindication to post-exposure prophylaxis as it is considered 100% fatal.
  • Rabies vaccine can be given in pregnancy, HIV, to Immunocompromised, infants, and children.

Animal bites even if from a vaccinated animal, PEP should be considered. (Statement 5)


Re-exposure: Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is not mandatory for all re-exposures, administered if no history of previous vaccination status with immunoglobulin. (Statement 4)

question: All are true regarding rabies vaccine except?

correctAnswer: A. Mass vaccination of domestic dogs and cats
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most effective step to control the disease and prevent its transmission is Mass vaccination of domestic dogs and cats.

  1. Prevents Transmission at the Source: Many of these animals can be vaccinated, achieving herd immunity. This means that even if an occasional rabid animal enters the community, it will be less likely to transmit the disease.
  2. Cost-Effective and Sustainable
  3. Ethical Considerations: Culling of stray animals is considered to be unethical (Option B).

Quarantine (Option C) can be impractical and resource-intensive for managing suspected rabid animals. In the case of exotic animals quarantine period are implemented.

Public awareness campaigns (Option D) are important but are secondary to controlling the disease at its source through vaccination.

Explanation:

Hence, API = 400*1000/5000 = 80 per 1000 population.

Annual parasite incidence is the estimated number of confirmed malaria cases ( by smear microscopy) per year in a population.

Regions with API >2 per 1000 population have been classified as high-risk zones. Vector control strategies should be undertaken.

The NVBDCP uses API to categorize states and union territories (UTs) into four groups for malaria elimination:

  • Category 0: States and UTs with no indigenous cases.
  • Category 1: States and UTs with an API below 1 case per 1,000 people at risk
  • Category 2: States and UTs with an API below 1 case per 1,000 people at risk, but some districts have an API of 1 case or more per 1,000 people at risk

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Management of Filariasis

Treatment

Triple Drug therapy

  • Diethylcarbamazine (DEC): 6 mg/kg/day for 12 days +
  • Albendazole stat (400 mg: > 2 years, 200mg: < 2 years ) +
  • Ivermectin (150-200 mcg/Kg)

Acute dermato-lymphangio adenitis (ADLA):

  • Analgesics: Paracetamol
  • Antibiotics: no anti filarial drug
    • Uncomplicated: Amoxicillin, erythromycin
    • Severe: IV Penicillin

Prevention
  • Annual Mass Drug Administration (MDA):
    • Yearly triple drug therapy with DEC, albendazole and ivermectin
    • Coverage: >65% for 5-6 years
    • Lymphatic filariasis elimination strategy: microfilariae rate <1%
    • Conduct a filarial survey in all age groups before starting MDA and a TAS (transmission assessment survey) among the 6-7 years age group after MDA
    • Stop MDA if TAS < 2% followed by post-MDA surveillance with 2 more rounds of TAS
  • DEC Medication Salts:
    • 1- 4 gms of DEC is added per 1kg of salt in Maharashtra and Lakshadweep Islands
  • Vector Control (Integrated vector management):
    • Anti Larval: Larvicidal oil (pyrosene oil, fenthion, temephos)
    • Anti-adult: DDT (6 monthly), lindane, malathion (quarterly)
  • Aquatic plant removal: Water hyacinths, Pistia plants


Reference:

Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 317-321

Explanation:

Leptospirosis is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, calf tenderness, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, and a history of exposure to flooded rice paddies.

Leptospirosis

Agent
  • Leptospira interrogans (zoonotic bacteria)

Reservoir
  • Rodents (Ratus norvegicus, Mus musculus) and domestic animals

Source
  • Direct contact or contamination with excreta, urine of infected animals.

At risk individuals
  • Males 20-45 years (most common)
  • Urine-contaminated mud(Soil) or water
    • Sports: rafting, fishing and swimming
    • Rice field workers, sewer workers, animal handlers

Mode of transmission
  • Direct contact: Urine through skin abrasion
  • Indirect contact: Contact of broken skin with soil, water, vegetation
  • Droplet infection: Inhalation while milking cows.

Incubation
  • 4-20 days

Diagnosis
  • Clinical features
  • Darkfield examination: Thin and motile spirochete.
  • IgM ELISA: High sensitivity
  • Labs: Elevated liver enzymes, increased bilirubin, thrombocytopenia

Dengue (Option A) typically presents with high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, rash, and bleeding tendencies with laboratory tests showing thrombocytopenia.

Malaria (Option B) presents with periodic fevers, jaundice, headache, and muscle pain. A blood smear shows intraerythrocytic plasmodium parasites.

Hepatitis A (Option D) causes jaundice and elevated liver enzymes but it is transmitted through contaminated food and water and is less associated with working in flooded paddies.

The incubation period is the interval between the infective mosquito bite and the first appearance of clinical symptoms.

  • Among the human malaria parasites, Plasmodium falciparum has the shortest incubation period, typically about 12 days (range: 9-14 days), making it the earliest to present clinically after infection.
  • Its rapid onset is clinically important because falciparum malaria can progress quickly and is associated with severe complications such as cerebral malaria, severe anemia, and multiorgan involvement.

Plasmodium vivax (Option A): This species typically has an incubation period of about 14 days (range: 8-17 days), which is longer than P. falciparum. Some strains may show delayed incubation for several months due to dormant liver hypnozoites.

Plasmodium malariae (Option C): This species has the longest incubation period among the common human malarial parasites, averaging 28 days (range: 18-40 days).

Plasmodium ovale (Option D): This species usually has an incubation period of about 17 days (range: 16-18 days), which is longer than that of P. falciparum.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Anopheles fluviatilis is the principal malaria vector in hilly areas, forests, and forest fringes, especially in many eastern and central parts of India.

  • It is an important vector in forest malaria because these ecological zones favor persistent malaria transmission and often have a higher burden of Plasmodium falciparum infection.
  • Its epidemiological importance is greatest in tribal and forested regions, where malaria control is more difficult because of difficult terrain, scattered populations, and limited health access.
  • Anopheles fluviatilis is considered a highly efficient vector because it commonly feeds on humans in endemic zones, contributing significantly to sustained transmission in forest-fringe communities.
  • These regions are major targets for malaria surveillance, early diagnosis, insecticide-based vector control, and indoor residual spraying.

Urban areas (Option A): Anopheles stephensi is the principal vector in urban and industrial areas and is classically associated with malaria transmission in cities.

Rural areas (Option B): Anopheles culicifacies is the major vector in rural and peri-urban plains and is the most important rural malaria vector in India.

Coastal areas (Option D): Coastal malaria is associated with vectors such as Anopheles sundaicus / Anopheles epiroticus complex, which are adapted to coastal and brackish-water environments, unlike Anopheles fluviatilis.

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 307

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Duffy-negative red blood cells confer natural resistance to Plasmodium vivax infection, because P. vivax classically requires the Duffy blood group antigen (DARC/ACKR1 receptor) on the RBC surface to invade erythrocytes.

  • The parasite attaches through its Duffy-binding protein (DBP), and in the absence of this receptor, invasion is blocked.
  • This genetic trait is common in many populations of West and Central Africa, explaining the historically low prevalence of P. vivax malaria in these regions.
  • This is a classic example of host genetic protection against malaria.

Plasmodium falciparum (Option A): Resistance to P. falciparum is associated with traits such as sickle cell trait, thalassemia, and G6PD deficiency, not Duffy negativity.

Plasmodium malariae (Option B): P. malariae does not depend on the Duffy antigen for RBC invasion, so Duffy negativity does not confer protection.

Plasmodium ovale (Option D): P. ovale invades RBCs independently of the Duffy antigen and is not blocked by Duffy-negative status.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 309

Explanation:

Quinine is the drug of choice for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria during the first trimester of pregnancy, as recommended in Indian malaria treatment guidelines.

  • ACTs are avoided during early pregnancy because of concerns regarding fetal safety during organogenesis.
  • Quinine is typically given for 7 days, and in many treatment protocols, it is combined with clindamycin to improve cure rates and reduce treatment failure.
  • In the second and third trimesters, Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) is recommended instead, as it is considered safer after the first trimester.

Artemether-Lumefantrine (Option A): This ACT is generally avoided in the first trimester and is recommended mainly in the second and third trimesters.

Chloroquine (Option B): Although safe in pregnancy, chloroquine is not the drug of choice for falciparum malaria because most P. falciparum strains are chloroquine-resistant.

Primaquine (Option C): Primaquine is contraindicated throughout pregnancy because it may cause hemolysis in a G6PD-deficient fetus.

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 314

explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Cardiac disease is not a standard contraindication to primaquine use.

  • Primaquine is the classical drug used for radical cure of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale malaria because it eliminates dormant liver hypnozoites in the liver.
  • Its major serious adverse effect is hemolytic anaemia, especially in individuals with impaired red cell protective mechanisms.
  • G6PD deficiency (Option A) is the most important contraindication because primaquine can precipitate severe acute hemolysis in these patients.
  • Primaquine is also contraindicated during pregnancy (Option B), since fetal G6PD status cannot be reliably determined and fetal hemolysis may occur.
  • It is contraindicated in infants (Option D) under 1 year as recommended in malaria treatment guidelines because of increased susceptibility to hemolytic complications.


Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 314

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Vector control is the principal community-level strategy for reducing malaria transmission in endemic areas, because it directly targets the Anopheles mosquito, the essential vector responsible for spreading malaria between humans.

  • In the absence of an effective, widely deployed vaccine, reducing mosquito density, survival, and human-vector contact remains the most practical and effective public health approach.
  • Major vector control measures include insecticide-treated bed nets, indoor residual spraying, larval source management, and environmental modification.
  • These interventions reduce mosquito lifespan below the period required for parasite development, thereby interrupting transmission.

Chemoprophylaxis (Option A): Chemoprophylaxis is mainly used for travellers and selected high-risk groups, not as a mass community control strategy in endemic populations.

Case detection (Option C): Early diagnosis and prompt treatment reduce morbidity and help lower parasite reservoirs, but they do not replace vector control as the primary transmission-reduction strategy.

Health education (Option D): Health education improves community participation and promotes preventive behaviours, but by itself does not directly interrupt malaria transmission.



Reference:

Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 28th Edition, Page 310
question: Which is the principal community-level strategy for reducing malaria transmission in endemic areas?

correctAnswer: B. Ensuring proper use of insecticide-treated mosquito nets
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Roll Back Malaria (RBM) partnership, launched in 1998 by WHO, UNICEF, UNDP, and the World Bank, aimed to reduce global malaria morbidity and mortality by scaling up effective, evidence-based interventions.

  • One of its central pillars was the widespread promotion and correct use of insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs/LLINs), which reduce human-mosquito contact and significantly lower malaria transmission.
  • RBM also emphasised early diagnosis and prompt treatment, malaria prevention during pregnancy, and indoor residual spraying as part of integrated malaria control.

Mass drug administration (Option A): RBM focused on targeted diagnosis and treatment rather than universal mass drug administration as a routine core strategy.

Eradication of Anopheles mosquitoes (Option C): RBM aimed at malaria control and burden reduction, not complete eradication of the mosquito species.

Mandatory quarantine (Option D): Malaria is not controlled through quarantine; prevention depends on vector control, diagnosis, and treatment.

The extrinsic incubation period (EIP) is the time taken after a mosquito ingests dengue virus from an infected human until the virus replicates and reaches the mosquito’s salivary glands, making the mosquito capable of transmitting infection.

  • In Aedes aegypti, this period is typically 8-10 days under tropical conditions, though it may vary with temperature.
  • Higher ambient temperatures shorten the EIP, while lower temperatures prolong it.
  • This incubation period is crucial in dengue transmission dynamics because only mosquitoes surviving beyond this period become infective.

  • The most important and lifesaving intervention is early and judicious intravenous fluid therapy with isotonic crystalloids (normal saline or Ringer lactate) to maintain effective circulation and prevent progression to shock.
  • Fluid therapy should be carefully titrated based on clinical status, hematocrit trends, and urine output, and is usually required for 24-48 hours during the plasma leakage phase.

Platelet transfusion (Option A): Not indicated routinely; given only in severe bleeding or very low platelet counts with clinical risk, not based on platelet count alone.
